Let $\P$ be a probability measure on
\gbmarginpar{Removed ``the space''
$(\OmegaEd,\sFEd)$,
and let $(T_i,\sG_i)_{i=0}^n$
be an extended partition.
Then there exists a unique measure
$\Pc$ satisfying
\bea
\Pc[A]&=&\P[A],\quad A\in\sH_i,
\,\,i=0,1,\dots,n+1,\label{3.2}\\
\Pc\big[B\,\big|\,\sFEd_{T_i}\big]
&=&
\P\big[B\,\big|\,\sG_i\big],\quad
B\in\sH_{i+1},\,\,i=0,1,\dots,n.\label{3.3}
\eea
We interpret (\ref{3.3}) to mean that
every $\P$-version of
$\P[B\,|\,\sG_i]$ is a $\Pc$-version of
$\Pc[B\,|\,\sFEd_{T_i}]$.
\et

\begin{example}[Simple concatenated
measure]\label{SimpExPart1}
{\rm
Let $\sE=\{0\}$, so that
$\Omega^{\sE,1}$ is isomorphic to $C_0^1$.
Then $\sF^{\sE,1}_0$ is the trivial
$\sigma$-algebra $\{\emptyset,C_0^1\}$.
We consider the extended
\gbmarginpar{I changed $\Pi=(T_i,\sG_i)_{i=1}^{0}$
  to $\Pi=(T_i,\sG_i)_{i=0}^{1}$
partition $\Pi=(T_i,\sG_i)_{i=0}^{1}$
with $\sG_0=\sG_1=\{\emptyset,C_0^1\}$
and $T_0=0$, $T_1=1$, and, by convention,
$T_2=\infty$.  Then $\sH_0=\sF^{\sE,1}_0$,
$\sH_1=\sF^{\sE,1}_1=\sigma(X(t), 0\leq t\leq 1)$,
and $\sH_2=\sigma(X(t)-X(1), t\geq 1)$.
We define four elements of $C_0^1$
\gbmarginpar{Changed $\omega^1(t)=0$ to $\omega^0(t)=0$.
by
$\omega^0(t)=0$, $\omega^1(t)=t$,
$\omega^2(t)=t\wedge 1$ and $\omega^3(t)=(t-1)^+$
for $t\geq 0$.
Let $\delta^i$ be the probability measure
on $C_0^1$ assigning probability $1$
to $\omega^i$, and set
$\P=(\delta^0+\delta^1)/2$.
The sets
\gbmarginpar{Added a little more space before each $\forall$.}
$$
A_0=
\{x\in C_0^1:x(t)=0\;\;\forall t\in[0,1] \}
\mbox{ and }
A_1=
\{x\in C_0^1:x(t)=t\;\;\forall t\in[0,1]\}
$$
are in $\sH_1=\sF^{\sE,1}_1$
and $\P(A_0)=\P(A_1)=\frac12$.
According to (\ref{3.2}), we must also have
$\Pc(A_0)=\Pc(A_1)=\frac12$.
The sets
\beas
B_0
&=&
\{x\in C_0^1:x(t)-x(1)=0\;\;\forall t\in[1,\infty)\},\\
B_1
&=&
\{x\in C_0^1:x(t)-x(1)=t-1\;\;\forall t\in[1,\infty)\}
\eeas
are in $\sH_2$, and
\gbmarginpar{I reversed the order of the equation.
(\ref{3.3}) implies that
$$
\Pc[B_0\,|\,\sF^{\sE,1}_1]
=\P[B_0\,|\,\sG_1]
=\P[B_0]
=\frac12.
$$
Integrating this equation over $A_1$
with respect to $\Pc$,
we see that
\gbmarginpar{I reversed the order of $A_1$ and $B_0$.
$$
\frac14=\Pc(A_1\cap B_0)=\Pc(\omega^2).
$$
Considering all combinations of $A_j$
and $B_k$, we conclude that
$\Pc(\omega^i)=\frac14$ for $i=0,1,2,3$,
i.e., $\Pc=(\delta_0+\delta_1+\delta_2+\delta_3)/4$.
$\endproof$
}
\end{example}

The remainder of this subsection is devoted
\gbmarginpar{This paragraph has changed significantly.  I removed the
  $\oplus$ notation, so we only use $\otimes$.  This makes everything
  sync up with the notation in Stroock and Varadhan and allows us to
  abbreviate the proof of Prop. 4.6.
to the proof of Theorem \ref{T3.3}.  Let $\frakC^d$ denote the Borel
$\sigma$-field in $C^d$ and let $\frakC_0^d$ denote the trace
$\sigma$-field in $C_0^d$.  We first concatenate a deterministic
initial path and a probability measure at a deterministic time.  Given
a fixed point $\omegabar=(\ebar,\xbar)\in\OmegaEd$, a time $t \geq 0$,
and a probability measure $\Q$ on $(\OmegaEd,\sFEd)$, let
$\Psi_{\omegabar,t}\colon \OmegaEd\rightarrow\OmegaEd$ denote the
function
\begin{equation} \label{eq:1}
  \Psi_{\omegabar,t}(e,x)=\bigl(\ebar,\;\nabla(\xbar,t)+x-\nabla(x,t)\bigr),
\end{equation}
and set $\delta_{\omegabar}\otimes_t\Q =
\Q\circ\Psi^{-1}_{\omegabar,t}$.  The reader can easily check that the
measure $\delta_{\omegabar}\otimes_t\Q$ is uniquely determined by the
properties
\begin{gather}
  \label{eq:2}
  (\delta_{\omegabar}\otimes_t\Q)
    [E = \ebar, X_s = \xbar(s) \;\; \forall s \leq t] = 1,
  \\
  \label{eq:3}
  (\delta_{\omegabar}\otimes_t\Q)[\Delta(X, t) \in A]
    = \Q[\Delta(X, t) \in A], \quad \forall A \in \frakC_0^d.
\end{gather}
If $\Q[X_t=\xbar(t)] = 1$, $\calE = \R^d$, and we identify $\OmegaEd$
with $C^d$ in the natural way, then this notation reduces to the
construction given in Lemma 6.1.1 of \cite{SV2}.


In the next step, we concatenate an initial probability
\gbmarginpar{I added this sentence.
measure and a probability kernel at a stopping time.

\begin{definition}\label{D3.4}
Let $(\Omega',\sF')$ and $(\Omega'',\sF'')$ be
\gbmarginpar{I modified this definition.  There is
  no reason to mention $\sG'$.
measurable spaces.
We say that a function
$Q\colon\Omega'\times\sF''\rightarrow[0,1]$
is a
{probability kernel from $(\Omega',\sF')$ to
$(\Omega'',\sF'')$} provided
\bdes
\item[(a)]
$Q(\omega',A'')$ is a $\sF'$-measurable
function of $\omega'\in\Omega'$
for each $A''\in\sF''$,
\item[(b)]
$Q(\omega',\cdot)$ is a probability measure on
$(\Omega'',\sF'')$ for each $\omega'\in\Omega'$.
\edes
\end{definition}

\gbmarginpar{I removed a descriptive paragraph
  which described the (now gone) $\oplus$ construction
  in words.  I believe the sentence prior to the previous
  definition gives essentially the same information.
  Whereas $\oplus$ takes a measure on $C_0^d$ as its second argument,
  $\otimes$ takes a measure on $\OmegaEd$ and has the differencing
  built in.

\bp\label{P3.5}
Let $\P$ be a probability measure on
$(\OmegaEd,\sFEd)$, let $T$ be a finite (for every
$\omega$) $\{\sFEd_t\}_{t\geq 0}$-stopping time,
and let $Q$ be a probability
kernel from $(\OmegaEd,\sFEd_T)$ to
$(\OmegaEd,\sFEd)$.  Then there exists a
unique probability measure $\P\otimes_TQ$ on
$(\OmegaEd,\sFEd)$ such that
\bdes
\item[(a)]
$\P\otimes_TQ[A]=\P[A],\quad A\in\sFEd_T$,
\item[(b)]
the random variable
$\omega\mapsto\big(\delta_{\omega}
\otimes_{T(\omega)}
Q(\omega,\cdot)\big)[F]$
is a version of the conditional probability
$(\P\otimes_TQ)[F\,|\,\sFEd_T]$ for all $F\in\sFEd$.
\edes
\ep

\noi {\sc Proof:}
\gbmarginpar{The statement and proof of Prop 4.6 have changed.
  It is now shorter and uses the
  result from Stroock and Varadhan in a effort to address the
  referee's concerns about rederiving known results.
When the initial condition $Q(\omegabar,
\{X_{T(\omegabar)}=X_{T(\omegabar)}(\omegabar)\}) = 1$ holds for each
$\omegabar \in \OmegaEd$, the result follows in the same way as
Theorem~6.1.2 of \cite{SV2}.  To handle the general case, we modify
the initial segment of each path to ensure that the proper
initial condition holds.  Let $\Psi_{\omegabar,t}$ be defined as in
\eqref{eq:1} and set $\Qhat(\omegabar, \cdot\,) = Q(\omegabar,
\cdot\,) \circ \Psi^{-1}_{\omegabar, T(\omegabar)}$.  The map
$(\omegabar, \omega) \mapsto \Psi_{\omegabar, T(\omegabar)}(\omega)$
is $\sFEd_T \otimes \sFEd / \sFEd$-measurable, so $\Qhat$ is a
probability kernel from $(\OmegaEd,\sFEd_T)$ to $(\OmegaEd,\sFEd)$.
It follows from the definition of $\Psi$ that $\Qhat(\omegabar,
\{X^{T(\omegabar)}=X^{T(\omegabar)}(\omegabar)\}) = 1$ for each $\omegabar \in
\OmegaEd$, so we may apply the previous case to conclude that there
exists a unique measure $\P\otimes_T \widehat Q$ such that (a) and (b)
hold when $Q$ is replaced with $\widehat Q$.  But the operator $\omega
\mapsto \Psi_{\omegabar,t}(\omega)$ is idempotent, so
$\delta_{\omegabar} \otimes_{T(\omegabar)} Q(\omegabar,\cdot) =
\delta_{\omegabar} \otimes_{T(\omegabar)} \widehat Q(\omegabar,\cdot)$
for each $\omegabar \in \OmegaEd$, and $\P\otimes_T Q = \P\otimes_T
\widehat Q$ is in fact the unique measure which satisfies (a) and (b).
$\endproof$

\vspace{\baselineskip}
We now begin concatenating probability measures.
\gbmarginpar{I added a sentence (and baselineskip) before Cor. 4.7.

\bcor[Two-fold concatenation]\label{C3.6}
Let $\P_1$ and $\P_2$ be probability measures
on $\OmegaEd$, let $T$ be a finite (for every
$\omega$)  $\{\sFEd_t\}_{t\geq 0}$-stopping time,
let $\sG$ be a sub-$\sigma$-field of $\sFEd_T$,
and assume that $\P_1|{\sG}\ll\P_2|_{\sG}$.
Then there exists a unique measure, denoted
$\P_1\otimes_{T,\sG}\P_2$, such that
\bdes
\item[(a)]
$\P_1\otimes_{T,\sG}\P_2[A]=\P_1[A],
\quad A\in\sFEd_T,$
\item[(b)]
for every set $B\in\sG\vee\sigma(\Delta(X,T))$,
every version of $\P_2[B\,|\,\sG]$ is a
version of
$(\P_1\otimes_{T,\sG}\P_2)[B\,|\,\sFEd_T]$,
\item[(c)]
if $\P_1$ and $\P_2$ agree on  $\sG$, then
$\P_1\otimes_{T,\sG}\P_2$ and $\P_2$ agree on
$\sG\vee\sigma(\Delta(X,T))$.
\edes
\ecor

\noi
{\sc Proof:}
Because $\OmegaEd$ is a Polish space, there
\gbmarginpar{The first two paragraphs of this proof
  are modified (and slightly shorter).
exists a $\sG$-measurable probability kernel $Q$ from
$(\OmegaEd,\sFEd)$ to $(\OmegaEd,\sFEd)$ such that for every
$F\in\sFEd$, $Q(\cdot,F)$ is a version of $\P_2[F\,|\,\sG]$
(\cite{SV2}, Theorem 1.1.6).  Using Proposition \ref{P3.5}, we define
$\P_1\otimes_{T,\sG}\P_2\define\P_1\otimes_TQ$.  Property (a) of the
corollary is property (a) of Proposition \ref{P3.5}.

Given $\omega \in \OmegaEd$ and $F \in \sFEd$,
set $\Qhat(\omega, F) = (\delta_\omega
\otimes_{T(\omega)}Q(\omega,\cdot))[F]$.  Property (b) of Proposition
\ref{P3.5} asserts that $\Qhat(\cdot, F)$ is version of
$(\P\otimes_TQ)[F\,|\,\sFEd_T]$ for all $F \in \sFEd$.
Galmarino's Test (see \cite{DM}
Theorem~IV.100) remains valid for the filtered space $(\OmegaEd,\sFEd,
\{\sFEd_t\}_{t\geq 0})$, so $\Qhat(\omega, A \cap F) = \ind_A(\omega)
\Qhat(\omega, F)$ for all $\omega \in \OmegaEd$, $A \in \sFEd_T$, and
$F \in \sFEd$ by \eqref{eq:2}.  If $B$ takes the form
$B=A\cap\{\Delta(X,T)\in D\}$ with $A\in\sG$ and $D\in\frakC_0^d$,
then \eqref{eq:3} implies
\begin{equation}
  \label{eq:4}
  \Qhat(\cdot, B)
  = \ind_A Q(\cdot, \{\Delta(X, T) \in D\})
    = \P_2[B\,|\,\sG], \quad \P_2\mbox{-a.s.}
\end{equation}
It then follows from Dynkin's $\pi$-$\lambda$
theorem that \eqref{eq:4} holds for
all $B \in \sG\vee\sigma(\Delta(X,T))$.
From (a) we have
$\P_1\otimes_{T,\sG}\P_2|_{\sG}=\P_1|_{\sG}$,
and  we have assumed
$\P_1|_{\sG}\ll\P_2|_{\sG}$,
so the fact that $\Qhat(\cdot, B)$ is a version
of both $(\P_1\otimes_{T,\sG}\P_2)[B\,|\,\sFEd_T]$
and $\P_2[B\,|\,\sG]$
implies that every version of
$\P_2[B\,|\,\sG]$ is also a version of
$(\P_1\otimes_{T,\sG}\P_2)[B\,|\,\sFEd_T]$.

For (c), assume that $\P_1$ and $\P_2$ agree
\gbmarginpar{The remainder of the proof (and section) is unchanged.
on $\sG$.  Property (a) implies that
$\P_1|_{\sG}=(\P_1\otimes_{T,\sG}\P_2)|_{\sG}$,
and hence
$\P_2|_{\sG}=\P_1\otimes_{T,\sG}\P_2|_{\sG}$.
For $B\in\sG\vee\sigma(\Delta(X,T))$,
we have from (b) that
$\P_2[B\,|\,\sG]
=(\P_1\otimes_{T,\sG}\P_2)[B\,|\,\sG]$,
and we can integrate both sides over $\OmegaEd$
with respect to
$\P_2|_{\sG}=\P_1\otimes_{T,\sG}\P_2|_{\sG}$
to obtain (c).

Uniqueness of $\P_1\otimes_{T,\sG}\P_2$
follows from the fact that (b) specifies this
measure on $\sG\vee\sigma(\Delta(X,T))$
conditioned on $\sFEd_T$, up to
$\P_2|_{\sG}$-equivalence.  Furthermore, (a)
specifies this measure to be $\P_1$ on $\sFEd_T$,
and hence on $\sG$.
But $\P_1\ll\P_2$, and hence the integral
in the equation
$(\P_1\otimes_{T,\sG}\P_2)[B]
=\int_{\OmegaEd}\P_2[B\,|\,\sG]\,d\P_1$ for
$B\in\sG\vee\sigma(\Delta(X,T))$
is well defined.
We see then that properties (a) and (b)
specify the measure $\P_1\otimes_{T,\sG}\P_2$ on
$\sG\vee\sigma(\Delta(X,T))$
and on $\sFEd_T$.  These
two $\sigma$-fields generate $\sFEd$, and thus
the measure is uniquely determined
on $\sFEd$ by properties (a) and (b).
$\endproof$

\bp[Three-fold concatenation]\label{P3.7}
Let $\P_1$, $\P_2$ and $\P_3$ be probability
measures on $\OmegaEd$ and let $0\leq S\leq T$ be
finite (for every $\omega$)
$\{\sFEd_t\}_{t\geq 0}$-stopping times.  Let
$\sG$ be a sub-$\sigma$-field of $\sFEd_S$
and let $\sH$ be a sub-$\sigma$-field of
$\sG\vee\sigma(\Delta(X^T,S))$, which is a
sub-$\sigma$-field of $\sFEd_T$.  Assume that
$T-S$ is
$\sG\vee\sigma(\Delta(X,S))$-measurable.
If $\P_1|_{\sG}\ll\P_2|_{\sG}$ and
$\P_2|_{\sH}\ll\P_3|_{\sH}$, then
\bdes
\item[(a)]
$\P_1|_{\sG}\ll
(\P_2\otimes_{T,\sH}\P_3)|_{\sG}$,
\item[(b)]
$(\P_1\otimes_{S,\sG}\P_2)|_{\sH}
\ll\P_3|_{\sH}$,
\edes
so that both
$\P_1\otimes_{S,\sG}(\P_2\otimes_{T,\sH}\P_3)$
and
$(\P_1\otimes_{S,\sG}\P_2)\otimes_{T,\sH}\P_3$
are defined, and
\bdes
\item[(c)]
$\P_1\otimes_{S,\sG}(\P_2\otimes_{T,\sH}\P_3)
=(\P_1\otimes_{S,\sG}\P_2)\otimes_{T,\sH}\P_3$.
\edes
\ep

\noi
{\sc Proof:}
We simplify notation by writing
$\P_{12}=\P_1\otimes_{S,\sG}\P_2$,
$\P_{23}=\P_2\otimes_{T,\sH}\P_3$,
$\P_{1,23}=\P_1\otimes_{S,\sG}
(\P_2\otimes_{T,\sH}\P_3)$, and
$\P_{12,3}=(\P_1\otimes_{S,\sG}\P_2)
\otimes_{T,\sH}\P_3$.
For (a), we note from Corollary \ref{C3.6}(a)
that $\P_{23}$ agrees with $\P_2$ on $\sFEd_T$,
and hence on $\sG$.  Property (a) follows from
$\P_1|_{\sG}\ll\P_2|_{\sG}$.
For (b), let $A\in\sH$ satisfy $\P_3[A]=0$.  By
assumption, we also have $\P_2[A]=0$, and hence
$0$ is a version of $\P_2[A\,|\,\sG]$.  Being in
$\sH$, $A$ is also in
$\sG\vee\sigma(\Delta(X,S))$, and according to
Corollary \ref{C3.6}(b), $0$ is a version of
$\P_{12}[A\,|\,\sFEd_S]$.  Therefore, $\P_{12}[A]=0$.

The collection of sets of the form
$A\cap B\cap C$, where
$A\in\sFEd_S$, $B\in\sigma(\Delta(X^T,S))$,
and $C\in\sigma(\Delta(X,T))$, is closed under
finite intersections and generates $\sFEd$.
Thus, to prove (c), it suffices to show
that the desired equation holds when both sides
are evaluated for a set of this form.  Let $A$,
$B$ and $C$ be as described, and let $G$ be
in $\sG$.  Let $Z$ be a version of
$\E_3[\ind_C\,|\,\sH]$ and $Y$ a version of
$\E_2[\ind_BZ\,|\,\sG]$.  Corollary \ref{C3.6}(b)
implies that $Z$ is a version of
$\P_{23}[C\,|\,\sFEd_T]$.    This combined with
Corollary \ref{C3.6}(a) implies
$$
\E_{23}[\ind_GY]
=\E_2[\ind_GY]
=\E_2[\ind_{G\cap B}Z]
=\E_{23}[\ind_{G\cap B}Z]
=\E_{23}[G\cap B\cap C].
$$
We see then that
$Y=\E_2[\ind_B\E_3[\ind_C\,|\,\sH]\,|\,\sG]$
is a version of $\E_{23}[\ind_{B\cap C}\,|\,\sG]$,
a fact we use along with repeated applications
of Corollary \ref{C3.6}(a), (b) and (c) in the
chain of equalities
\beas
\P_{1,23}[A\cap B\cap C]
&=&
\E_{1,23}\Big[\ind_A\E_{1,23}[\ind_{B\cap C}\,|\,
\sFEd_S]\big]\\
&=&
\E_{1,23}
\big[\ind_A\E_{23}[\ind_{B\cap C}\,|\,\sG]\big]\\
&=&
\E_{1,23}\Big[\ind_A\E_2
\big[\ind_B\E_3[\ind_C\,|\,\sH]\,\big|\,\sG\big]\Big]\\
&=&
\E_1\Big[\ind_A\E_2
\big[\ind_B\E_3[\ind_C\,|\,\sH]\,\big|\,\sG\big]\Big]\\
&=&
\E_{12}\Big[\ind_A\E_{12}\big[\ind_B\E_3
[\ind_C\,|\,\sH]\,\big|\,\sFEd_S\big]\Big]
\\
&=&
\E_{12}\big[\ind_{A\cap B}
\E_3[\ind_C\,|\,\sH]\big]\\
&=&
\E_{12,3}\big[\ind_{A\cap B}\E_{12,3}
[\ind_C\,|\,\sFEd_S]\big]\\
&=&
\P_{12,3}[A\cap B\cap C].\hspace{1.8in}\endproof
\eeas

\noi
{\sc Proof of Theorem \ref{T3.3}:}
Let $m$ satisfy $0\leq m\leq n-1$.
According to Definition \ref{D3.2},
$$
\sG_{m+1}\subset\sH_{m+1}
=\sG_m\vee
\sigma\big(\Delta(X^{T_{m+1}},T_m)\big)
\subset\sG_m\vee
\sigma\big(\Delta(X,T_m)\big).
$$
If $0\leq m\leq n-2$, we further have
$$
\sG_{m+2}\subset\sH_{m+2}=\sG_{m+1}\vee
\sigma\big(\Delta(X^{T_{m+2}},T_{m+1})\big)
\subset\sG_m\vee\sigma\big(\Delta(X,T_m)\big).
$$
Iterating this process, we obtain the relation
$\sG_{j}\subset\sG_m\vee
\sigma\big(\Delta(X,T_m)\big)$ for
$j=m,m+1,\dots,n$.
Consequently,
\be\label{3.10}
\sG_j\vee
\sigma\big(\Delta(X^{T_{j+1}},T_j)\big)
\subset\sG_m\vee
\sigma\big(\Delta(X,T_m)\big),\quad
0\leq m\leq j\leq n.
\ee

We now proceed by induction on $m$.
The induction hypothesis corresponding to $m$,
where $m=0,\dots,n$, is
the existence of a measure $\P^m$ such that
\bdes
\item[(i)]
$\P^m[A]=\P[A]$ for all $A\in\sH_i$ and
$0\leq i\leq n+1$,
\item[(ii)]
for $B\in\sH_{i+1}$ and $0\leq i\leq m-1$,
every $\P$-version of $\P[B\,|\,\sG_i]$ is a
$\P^m$-version of  $\P^m[B\,|\,\sFEd_{T_i}]$.
\edes
The base case is $\P^0=\P$, a case for which (i)
trivially holds and (ii) is vacuous.

Assume the induction hypothesis for some
integer $m$.
Because $\sG_{m}\subset\sH_{m}$ and the measures
$\P^m$ and $\P$ agree on $\sH_{m}$, we may
invoke Corollary \ref{C3.6} to define
$\P^{m+1}\define\P^m\otimes_{T_{m},\sG_{m}}\P$.
If $A\in\sH_j$ for some $j$, $0\leq j\leq m$,
then $A\in\sFEd_{T_{m}}$ and
$\P^{m+1}[A]=\P^{m}[A]=\P[A]$ by Corollary
\ref{C3.6}(a) and part (i) of the induction
hypothesis.  If $m\leq j\leq n$,
then (\ref{3.10}) implies
\be\label{HinG}
\sH_{j+1}\define\sG_j\vee\sigma
\big(\Delta(X^{T_{j+1}},T_j)\big)
\subset\sG_{m}\vee
\sigma\big(\Delta(X,T_{m})\big).
\ee
But Corollary \ref{C3.6}(c) implies that
$\P^{m+1}$ agrees with $\P$ on
$\sG_m\vee\sigma\big(\Delta(X,T_m)\big)$.
Hence, $\P^{m+1}$ satisfies (i).

For some $i$, $0\leq i\leq m-1$, let
$B\in\sH_{i+1}$ and $A\in\sFEd_{T_i}$ be given.
Suppose $Z$ is a version of $\P[B\,|\,\sG_i]$, so
that both $A\cap B$ and $\ind_AZ$ are
$\sFEd_{T_m}$-measurable (recall
(\ref{3.1a})).  Corollary
\ref{C3.6}(a) (used twice)
and part (ii) of the induction
hypothesis imply
$$
\E^{m+1}[\ind_AZ]=\E^m[\ind_AZ]=\P^m[A\cap B]
=\P^{m+1}[A\cap B],
$$
showing that $Z$ is a version of
$\P^{m+1}[B\,|\,\sFEd_{T_i}]$.  Finally, suppose
$B$ is in $\sH_{m+1}$, which is a
sub-$\sigma$-field of
$\sG_m\vee\sigma(\Delta(X,T_m))$.
Corollary \ref{C3.6}(b) says that every version
of $\P[B\,|\,\sG_m]$ is a version of
$\P^{m+1}[B\,|\,\sFEd_{T_m}]$.  This establishes
(ii) with $m+1$ replacing $m$.

The induction argument above constructs
$\P^{\otimes\Pi}\define\P^{n+1}$ that satisfies
(\ref{3.2}) and (\ref{3.3}).  To see that this
measure is unique, we show that (\ref{3.2}) and
(\ref{3.3}) determine its value on sets of the
form $\cap_{i=0}^{n+1}B_i$, where
$B_0\in\sFEd_0=\sH_0$
and
$B_{i+1}\in\sigma(\Delta(X^{T_{i+1}},T_i))
\subset\sH_{i+1}$
for $i=0,\dots,n$.  This collection of sets
is closed under finite intersections and
generates $\sFEd$.  For such a set, repeated
application of (\ref{3.3}), followed
by a final application of (\ref{3.2}), yields
\gbmarginpar{I removed the break in the following
  display because it all fits on one page now.
\bea
\lefteqn{
\P^{\otimes\Pi}\big[\cap_{i=0}^{n+1}B_i\big]}
\nonumber\\
&=&
\E^{n+1}\Big[\ind_{B_0}\E^{n+1}
\big[\ind_{B_1}\cdots
\E^{n+1}\big[
\ind_{B_n}\E^{n+1}[\ind_{B_{n+1}}\,|\,\sFEd_{T_n}]
\,\big|\,\sFEd_{T_{n-1}}\big]
\cdots\,\big|\,\sFEd_0\big]\Big]
\nonumber\\
&=&
\E^{n+1}\Big[\ind_{B_0}\E^{n+1}
\big[\ind_{B_1}\cdots
\E^{n+1}\big[
\ind_{B_n}\E[\ind_{B_{n+1}}\,|\,\sG_n]
\,\big|\,\sFEd_{T_{n-1}}\big]
\cdots\,\big|\,\sFEd_0\big]\Big]
\nonumber\\
&=&
\E^{n+1}\Big[\ind_{B_0}\E^{n+1}
\big[\ind_{B_1}\cdots
\E\big[\ind_{B_n}\E[\ind_{B_{n+1}}\,|\,\sG_n]
\big]\sG_{n-1}\big]
\cdots\,\big|\,\sFEd_0\big]\Big]
\nonumber\\
&\vdots&\nonumber\\
&=&
\E^{n+1}\Big[\ind_{B_0}\E\big[\ind_{B_1}\cdots
\E\big[\ind_{B_n}\E[\ind_{B_{n+1}}\,|\,\sG_n]
\,\big|\,\sG_{n-1}\big]
\cdots\,\big|\,\sG_0\big]\Big]\nonumber\\
&=&
\E\Big[\ind_{B_0}\E\big[\ind_{B_1}\cdots
\E\big[\ind_{B_n}\E[\ind_{B_{n+1}}\,|\,\sG_n]
\,\big|\,\sG_{n-1}\big]
\cdots\,\big|\,\sG_0\big]\Big].\label{3.11}
\eea
This concludes the proof of Theorem
\ref{T3.3}.$\endproof$

\br\label{R3.8}
{\rm
We see from the proof of Theorem \ref{T3.3} that
$$
\P^{\otimes\Pi}
=\P\otimes_{T_0,\sG_0}\P\otimes_{T_1,\sG_1}
\cdots
\otimes_{T_n,\sG_n}\P,
$$
where the associative property of Proposition
\ref{P3.7}(c) makes the grouping of the
$\otimes_{T_i,\sG_i}$ operators irrelevant.
Equation (\ref{3.11}) provides insight into
the nature of  $\P^{\otimes\Pi}$.  If $\sG_i$
is equal to $\sFEd_{T_i}$ for each $i$, then the
last iterated conditional expectation in
(\ref{3.11}) collapses to
$\P[\cap_{i=0}^{n+1}B_i]$, and
$\P^{\otimes\Pi}$ agrees with $\P$.  At the
other extreme, if $\sG_i$ is the trivial
$\sigma$-field $\{\emptyset,\OmegaEd\}$ for each
$i$, then this iterated conditional expectation
becomes $\prod_{i=0}^{n+1}\P[B_i]$, and
increments of the path fragments over
$[T_i,T_{i+1}]$ are  independent of one another
under $P^{\otimes\Pi}$ but have the same unconditional
distribution as under $\P$.
$\endproof$
}
\er

\subsection{Properties preserved by
concatenation}\label{SPropPres}

\bp\label{P3.9}
Let $\P$ be a probability measure and let
$(T_i,\sG_i)_{i=0}^n$ be an extended
partition on
\gbmarginpar{Added $\{\sFEd_t\}_{t\geq 0}$-adapted
$(\OmegaEd,\sFEd)$.  Let $A$ be an $\{\sFEd_t\}_{t\geq 0}$-adapted continuous
real-valued process on $\OmegaEd$, and assume
that $\Delta(A,T_i)$ is
$\sG_i\vee\sigma(\Delta(X,T_i))$-measurable for
$i=0,\dots,n$.
\bdes
\item[(a)]
The total variation of $A$ on $[0,\infty)$
is $\P$-almost surely finite if and only if
it is $\P^{\otimes\Pi}$-almost surely finite.
\item[(b)]
The process $A$ is $\P$-almost surely absolutely
continuous if and only if it
is $\P^{\otimes\Pi}$-almost surely absolutely continuous.
\edes
\ep

\noi
{\sc Proof:}
We set $\P^0=\P$ and
$\P^{i+1}=\P^i\otimes_{T_i,\sG_i}\P$,
$i=1,\dots,n$.
Then $\P^{\otimes\Pi}=\P^{n+1}$.
For (a), we proceed by induction
on $i=0,1,\dots,n$, assuming that
\bdes
\item[(a$\mbox{}_i$)]
the total variation of $A$ on $[0,\infty)$
is $\P$-almost surely finite if and only if
it is $\P^i$-almost surely finite.
\edes
On $\sFEd_{T_i}$, the probability measures $\P^i$
and $\P^{i+1}$ agree (Corollary \ref{C3.6}(a)),
and hence $A$ restricted
to $[0,T_i]$ is $\P^i$-a.s.\ of finite
variation if and only if $A$ restricted to
$[0,T_i]$ is $\P^{i+1}$-a.s.\ of finite
variation.  The variation of $A$
on subintervals in $[T_i,\infty)$ is a function
of $\Delta(A,T_i)$, which is
$\sG_i\vee\sigma(\Delta(X,T_i))$-measurable,
and on this $\sigma$-field, the measures $\P^i$
and $\P^{i+1}$ agree (Corollary \ref{C3.6}(c)).
Therefore,   $A$ restricted to $[T_i,\infty)$
is $\P^i$-a.s.\ of finite variation if and only
if $A$ restricted to $[T_i,\infty)$ is
$\P^{i+1}$-a.s.\ of finite variation.  We
conclude that
$A$ has finite total variation on $[0,\infty)$
$\P^i$-almost surely if and only if it has
finite total variation $\P^{i+1}$-almost surely.
Combining this with the
induction hypothesis (a$\mbox{}_i$),  we obtain
the induction hypothesis with $i+1$ replacing
$i$.

The continuous process $A$ is absolutely
continuous on $[0,\infty)$ if and only if it is
absolutely continuous on $[0,T_i]$ and
absolutely continuous on $[T_i,\infty)$.
Therefore, we can imitate the proof of (a)
to obtain (b).  $\endproof$

\bp\label{P3.10}
Let $\P$ be a probability measure and let
$(T_i,\sG_i)_{i=0}^n$ be an extended
partition on
\gbmarginpar{Added $\{\sFEd_t\}_{t\geq 0}$-adapted
$(\OmegaEd,\sFEd)$.  Let $A$ be an
$\{\sFEd_t\}_{t\geq 0}$-adapted continuous
$\R^d$-valued process on $\OmegaEd$
with $A_0=0$,
and assume that $\Delta(A,T_i)$ is
$\sG_i\vee\sigma(\Delta(X,T_i))$-measurable for
$i=0,\dots,n$.
Assume there exists a measurable $\R^d$-valued
process $\alpha$ such that the set
\be\label{3.14}
J(\omega)\define\left\{t\in[0,\infty):
\frac{\partial}{\partial t}A_t(\omega)
\mbox{ exists but is not equal to }
\alpha_t(\omega)\right\}
\ee
has Lebesgue measure zero for
$\P$-almost every and $\Pc$-almost every
$\omega\in\OmegaEd$.  Then
\be\label{3.15}
\P\left[A_t=\int_0^t\alpha_udu
\,\,\forall t\in[0,\infty)\right]=1
\ee
if and only if
\be\label{3.16}
\P^{\otimes\Pi}\left[A_t=\int_0^t\alpha_udu
\,\,\forall t\in[0,\infty)\right]=1.
\ee
When the equalities (\ref{3.15}) and
(\ref{3.16}) hold, we also have
\be\label{3.17}
\E\int_0^{S}f(\alpha_u)\,du
=\E^{\otimes\Pi}\int_0^{S}
f(\alpha_u)\,du
\ee
for every nonnegative, Borel-measurable function
$f\colon\R^d\rightarrow\R$ and
$\{\sFEd_t\}_{t\geq 0}$-stopping
time $S$ satisfying
$(S-T_i)^+\in\sG_i\vee\sigma(\Delta(X,T_i))$
for $i=0,\dots,n$.
\ep

\noi
{\sc Proof:}
Assume (\ref{3.15}).
Then each component of $A$ is $\P$-a.s.\ absolutely continuous.
Proposition \ref{P3.9} implies that the components of $A$ are
$\P^{\otimes\Pi}$-a.s.\ absolutely continuous
as well.  Therefore, for
$\P^{\otimes\Pi}$-almost every $\omega$, the set
$$
C(\omega)\define\left\{t\in[0,\infty):
\frac{\partial}{\partial t}A_t(\omega)
\mbox{ exists}\right\}
$$
has full Lebesgue measure, and by the assumption
about $J(\omega)$, the set
$$
D(\omega)\define\left\{t\in[0,\infty):
\frac{\partial}{\partial t}A_t(\omega)
\mbox{ exists and is equal to }
\alpha_t(\omega)\right\}
$$
also has full Lebesgue measure for
$\P^{\otimes\Pi}$-almost
every $\omega$.  This implies (\ref{3.16}).
This argument is reversible; (\ref{3.16})
implies (\ref{3.15}).

We now assume (\ref{3.15}) and (\ref{3.16}).
The
$\sG_i\vee\sigma(\Delta(X,T_i))$-measurability
of $\Delta(A,T_i)$ together with
the $\sFEd_{T_{i+1}}$-measurability of
$\Delta(A^{T_{i+1}},T_i)$
implies the
$\sH_{i+1}$-measurability of
$\Delta(A^{T_{i+1}},T_i)$.
Because $A$ is adapted and continuous,
$A_{T_i(\omega)+t}(\omega)
\ind_{\{0\leq t< T_{i+1}(\omega)-T_i(\omega)\}}$
is a jointly
$\sH_{i+1}\otimes{\cal B}[0,\infty)$-measurable
function of $(\omega,t)$, where $\sB[0,\infty)$
is the Borel $\sigma$-field on $[0,\infty)$ (recall
Remark \ref{R3.2}).  The same is then true for
the right-hand derivative
$\frac{\partial^+}{\partial t}A_{T_i(\omega)+t}
\ind_{\{0\leq t< T_{i+1}(\omega)
-T_i(\omega)\}}$, where we set this
right-hand derivative equal to
an arbitrary value whenever
the limit of the relevant difference quotient
does not exist.
By assumption, $(S-T_i)^+$ is also
$\sG_i\vee\sigma(\Delta(X,T_i))$-measurable.
Therefore,
$(T_{i+1}-T_i)\wedge(S-T_i)^+
=T_{i+1}\wedge S-T_i\wedge S$
is $\sH_{i+1}$-measurable.
But on each $\sH_{i+1}$, the measures $\P$
and $\P^{\otimes\Pi}$ agree, which implies
that for every nonnegative Borel-measurable
function $f\colon\R^d\rightarrow\R$,
$$
\E\int_0^{T_{i+1}\wedge S-T_i\wedge S}
f(\alpha_{T_i+u})\,du
=\E^{\otimes\Pi}
\int_0^{T_{i+1}\wedge S-T_i\wedge S}
f(\alpha_{T_i+u})\,du.
$$
Summing over $i=0,1,\dots,n$,
we obtain (\ref{3.17}).
$\endproof$

\bex[Example \ref{SimpExPart1} continued]
{\rm
Consider the extended partition and
probability measures $\P$ and $\Pc$
of Example \ref{SimpExPart1}.
We take $A=X$ so that $A_0=0$ and
$\Delta(A,T_i)$ is
$\sG_1\vee\sigma(\Delta(X,T_i))$-measurable
for $i=0,1$.
We define the adapted processes
\begin{align*}
  \alpha_t(\omega)
  &= \Bigl\{\limsup_{\epsilon\downarrow 0}
          0 \vee \frac{\omega(\epsilon)}{\epsilon} \wedge 1\Bigr\}
          \; \ind_{(0,\infty]}(t),
  \\
  \beta_t(\omega)
  &= \Bigl\{\limsup_{\epsilon\downarrow 0}
          0 \vee \frac{\omega(\epsilon)}{\epsilon} \wedge 1\Bigr\}
          \; \ind_{(0,1]}(t)
    + \Bigl\{\limsup_{\epsilon\downarrow 0}
          0 \vee \frac{\omega(1+\epsilon)-\omega(1)}{\epsilon} \wedge 1\Bigr\}
          \; \ind_{(1,\infty]}(t),
\end{align*}
and the sets $E = \{A_t=\int_0^t\alpha_u \, du \, \;\forall
t\in[0,\infty)\}$ and $F = \{A_t=\int_0^t\beta_u \, du \, \;\forall
t\in[0,\infty)\}$.  Then
we have $\P[E] = \P[F] = \Pc[F] = 1$, but
$\Pc[E] = 1/2$.

If we let $K(\omega)$ denote the set obtained by replacing $\alpha$
with $\beta$ in \eqref{3.14}, then we see that $K(\omega)$ is a
Lebesgue null set $\P$-almost surely and $\P^{\otimes\Pi}$-almost
surely.  On the other hand,
$J(\omega)$ defined by \eqref{3.14}
is a Lebesgue null set $\P$-almost surely, but has
strictly positive Lebesgue measure with
strictly positive
$\P^{\otimes\Pi}$-probability.  In particular,
we see that
\eqref{3.15} and \eqref{3.16} may
not be equivalent in this situation.
$\endproof$ }
\eex



\bcor\label{C3.11}
Let $\P$ be a probability measure on
$(\OmegaEd,\sFEd)$ and for each positive integer
$m$, let
$\Pi^m\define(T_i^m,\sG_i^m)_{i=0}^{N(m)}$
be an extended partition.  Let $A$ be an
\gbmarginpar{Added $\{\sFEd_t\}_{t\geq 0}$-adapted and abbreviated
  almost surely to a.s.
$\{\sFEd_t\}_{t\geq 0}$-adapted
continuous $\R^d$-valued process on
$\OmegaEd$ with $A_0=0$, and assume that
$T^m_i$ and $\Delta(A,T_i^m)$ are
$\sG_i^m\vee\sigma(\Delta(X,T_i^m))$-measurable
for $i=1,\dots,N(m)$ and $m=1,2\dots$.
Let $\alpha$ be a measurable $\R^d$-valued
process such that
$A_t=\int_0^t\alpha_udu$ for
{\em every} $t\geq 0$, $\P$-almost surely,
and assume that the set $J(\omega)$
defined by (\ref{3.14}) has Lebesgue
measure zero for {\em every} $\omega\in\OmegaEd$.
Finally, assume
\be\label{3.18b}
\E\int_0^t\|\alpha_u\|\,du<\infty,
\quad t\geq 0.
\ee
Then the following hold.
\bdes
\item[(a)]
For every $t\in[0,\infty)$,
$\alpha$ restricted to $[0,t]$ is uniformly
integrable with respect to
the collection of product measures
$\{\P^{\otimes\Pi^m}\times
\lambda_{[0,t]}\}_{m=1}^{\infty}$,
where $\lambda_{[0,t]}$ denotes Lebesgue
measure on $[0,t]$.
\item[(b)]
The collection of measures
$\{\P^{\otimes\Pi^m}\circ
A^{-1}\}_{m=1}^{\infty}$
on $C_0^d$ is tight.
\edes
\ecor

\noi
{\sc Proof:}
For (a), fix
$t\in[0,\infty)$.  Given $\epsilon>0$,
(\ref{3.18b}) guarantees that there exists
$M_\epsilon>0$ so large that
$\E\int_0^t\|\alpha_u\|
\ind_{\{\|\alpha_u\|\geq M_{\epsilon}\}}\,du
\leq\epsilon$.
Applying Proposition \ref{P3.10}
with $f(x)=\|x\|\ind_{\{\|x\|\geq M_{\epsilon}\}}$
and $S=t$, we obtain
$\E^{\otimes\Pi^m}
\int_0^t\|\alpha_u\|\ind_{\{\|\alpha_u\|\geq
M_{\epsilon}\}}\,du
\leq\epsilon$
for all $m$.

For (b) it
suffices to verify that for every
$\epsilon>0$, there exists a set
$\Omega_{\epsilon}\in\sFEd$ such that
$\P^{\otimes\Pi^m}(\Omega_{\epsilon})\geq
1-\epsilon$  for every $m$ and
\be\label{3.19b}
\lim_{\delta\downarrow 0}
\sup_{\omega\in \Omega_{\epsilon}}
\sup_{0\leq s\leq v\leq t\wedge (s+\delta)}
\|A_v(\omega)-A_s(\omega)\|=0,\quad t\geq 0.
\ee
Fix $\epsilon>0$ and let $\{t_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ be an
increasing sequence of positive numbers with
$\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}t_n=\infty$.
For fixed $n$, we construct $\Omega_n$ such that
$\Pcm(\Omega_n)\geq 1-2^{-n}\epsilon$ for every $m$ and
\be\label{3.20b}
\lim_{\delta\downarrow 0}\sup_{\omega\in\Omega_n}
\sup_{0\leq s\leq v\leq t_n\wedge(s+\delta)}
\|A_v(\omega)-A_s(\omega)\|=0.
\ee
Then $\Omega_{\epsilon}=\cap_{n=1}^{\infty}\Omega_n$
satisfies (\ref{3.19b}) and $\Pcm(\Omega_{\epsilon})\geq 1-\epsilon$
for every $m$.

We fix $n$ and construct $\Omega_n$ by working through the proof
of the Borel-Cantelli lemma.
For each positive integer $k$,
part (a) implies the existence of $\delta_k>0$
for which
$$
\E^{\otimes\Pi^m}\left[
\sup_{0\leq s\leq v\leq t_n\wedge(s+\delta_k)}
\|A_v-A_s\|\right]\leq
\E^{\otimes\Pi^m}
\left[\sup_{0\leq s\leq v\leq t_n\wedge(s+\delta_k)}
\int_s^v\|\alpha_u\|\,du\right]
\leq
2^{-2k}
$$
for all $m$.
We define
$F_k=
\left\{\sup_{0\leq s\leq v\leq t_n\wedge(s+\delta_k)}
\int_s^v\|\alpha_u\|\,du\geq 2^{-k}\right\}$,
and note from Chebyshev's inequality
that $\Pcm(F_k)\leq 2^{-k}$ for every $m$ and $k$.
Choose $j$ such that $2^{-(j-1)}\leq 2^{-n}\epsilon$ and
set $\Omega_n=\cap_{k\geq j}F_k^c$.  We have
$\Pcm(\Omega_n^c)\leq \sum_{k=j}^{\infty}\Pcm(F_k)
\leq 2^{-n}\epsilon$ for every $m$, as desired.
Also, $\omega\in\Omega_n$ implies that
$\sup_{0\leq s\leq v\leq t_n\wedge(s+\delta_k)}
\int_s^v\|\alpha_u\|\,du\leq 2^{-k}$
for all $k\geq j$, and hence (\ref{3.20b}) holds.
$\endproof$

\begin{definition}\label{D3.11}
Let $Y$ be an adapted continuous $\R^d$-valued process
defined on a filtered probability
\gbmarginpar{Moved filtration to third slot in tuple.
space $(\Omega,\sF,\{\sF_t\}_{t\geq 0},\P)$, let $B$
be an adapted continuous $\R^d$-valued process whose components
are of finite variation and for which $B_0=0$, and let
$C$ be an adapted continuous,
$d\times d$-matrix-valued process whose components
are of finite variation and for which $C_0=0$.
We further assume that outside a $\P$-null set
that does not depend on $s$ and $t$,
the increment $C_t-C_s$ is positive semi-definite whenever
$0\leq s<t<\infty$.
We say that {\em $Y$ is a semimartingale
with characteristic pair $(B,C)$} if the components of
$Y-B$ and $(Y-B)(Y-B)^{tr}-C$ are local martingales.
\end{definition}

\bp\label{P3.12}
Let $\P$ be a probability measure and let
$(T_i,\sG_i)_{i=0}^n$ be an extended partition
on $(\OmegaEd,\sFEd)$.
Let $Y$ be a continuous $\R^{d'}$-valued process ($d'$ may
be different from $d$),
and suppose that $Y$ is a semimartingale with
characteristic pair
$(B,C)$ under $\P$.  If $\Delta(Y,T_i)$, $\Delta(B,T_i)$
and $\Delta(C,T_i)$ are all $\sG_i\vee\sigma(\Delta(X,T_i))$-measurable
for $i=1,\dots,n$, then under $\P^{\otimes\Pi}$ the process
$Y$ is still a semimartingale with characteristic pair
$(B,C)$.
\ep

The proof of Proposition \ref{P3.12} depends on
\gbmarginpar{A lemma has been removed.}
some preliminary results.

\bl\label{L3.14}
Let $\P_1$ and $\P_2$ be probability measures on
$(\OmegaEd,\sFEd)$, and let $T$ be a finite (for every $\omega$)
$\{\sFEd_t\}_{t\geq 0}$-stopping time.
Let $M$ be a continuous
local martingale relative to $\{\sFEd_t\}_{t\geq 0}$
under $\P_1$ and $\P_2$.
Let $\sG$ be a sub-$\sigma$-field of $\sFEd_T$ such that
$\P_1|_{\sG}\ll\P_2|_{\sG}$ and assume that
$\Mhat\define\Delta(M,T)$ is
$\sG\vee\sigma(\Delta(X,T))$-measurable.
Then $(M_t,\sFEd_t)_{t\geq 0}$
is a continuous local martingale under
$\P_{12}\define\P_1\otimes_{T,\sG}\P_2$.
\el

\noi
{\sc Proof:}
\gbmarginpar{This proof has changed.  There used to be
  another lemma before this proposition, but it has been removed and
  moved into this proof.  This saves almost a page and is easier to
  read.
It is sufficient to show that $M^T$ and $M - M^T$ are both
$\P_{12}$-local martingales relative to $\{\sFEd_t\}_{t\geq 0}$.  As
$M^T$ is a $\P_1$-local martingale, $M^T$ is $\sFEd_T$-measurable, and
$\P_1$ and $\P_{12}$ agree on $\sFEd_T$, we may immediately conclude
that $M^T$ is a $\P_{12}$-local martingale.

For each integers $n > 0$, define the stopping time
$S^n\define\inf\{t\geq T:|M_t-M_T|\geq n\}$.  Then $M^{S_n} -
(M^{S_n})^T = M^{S_n} - M^T$ is bounded, and $\Delta(M^{S_n}, T)$ is
$\sG\vee\sigma(\Delta(X,T))$-measurable.  As a result, we may assume
without loss of generality that $M - M^T$ is a uniformly integrable
$\P_{2}$-martingale.

We now show that $\Mhat$ is a $\P_{12}$-martingale with respect to
the filtration $\sFhat_t = \sF_{T+t}$.  The process $\Mhat$ is clearly
$\{\sFhat_t\}_{t\geq 0}$-adapted, and it follows from the optional
sampling theorem that $\Mhat$ is a $\P_2$-martingale with respect to
the filtration $\{\sFhat_t\}_{t\geq 0}$.  For $0\leq s\leq t$,
$A\in\sFEd_T$, and $B\in\sigma(\Delta_r(X,T) : 0 \leq r \leq s)$, we
have from Corollary \ref{C3.6}(b) that \beas \E_{12}\big[\ind_{A\cap
  B}\big(\Mhat_t -\Mhat_s\big)\big] &=& \E_{12}\Big[\ind_A\E_{12}
\big[\ind_B\big(\Mhat_t
-\Mhat_s\big)\,\big|\,\sFEd_T\big]\Big]\\
&=& \E_{12}\Big[\ind_A \E_2\big[\ind_B\big(\Mhat_t
-\Mhat_s\big)\,\big|\,\sG\big]\Big]\\
&=& \E_{12}\left[\ind_A\E_2\Big[\ind_B \E_2\big[\Mhat_t
  -\Mhat_s\,\big|\,\sFhat_s\big]\,\Big|\,\sG\Big]\right] \,\,=\,\, 0,
\eeas where we have used the fact that $\Mhat$ is $\P_2$-martingale in
the last step.  Writing $X^{T+s}_t = X^T_t + \Delta_{0\vee (t-T)
  \wedge s}(X, T)$, we see that sets of the form $A\cap B$ generate
$\sFhat_s$.  It then follows from Dynkin's $\pi$-$\lambda$ theorem
that $\Mhat$ is $\P_{12}$-martingale relative to $\{\sFhat_t\}_{t\geq
  0}$.

To conclude the proof, we observe that
\gbmarginpar{$\sF_{r \vee T} \subset \sFhat_{(r-T)\vee
    0} \subset \sF_{(r \vee T)+}$, but it is not clear to me that $\sF_{r
    \vee T} = \sFhat_{(r-T)\vee 0}$ without right-continuity, so
  I don't even mention $\sFhat_{(r-T)\vee 0}$.
$(r - T)^+$ is a bounded $\{\sFhat_t\}_{t\geq 0}$-stopping time and
$\sF_r \subset \sFhat_{(r-T)\vee 0}$ for each $r \geq 0$.  Fixing $0
\leq s < t$ and $A \in \sF_s$, we have
\begin{equation*}
  \E_{12}[\ind_A (M_t - M^T_t) ]
  = \E_{12}[\ind_A \Mhat_{(t-T)\vee 0}]
  = \E_{12}[\ind_A \Mhat_{(s-T)\vee 0}]
  = \E_{12}[\ind_A (M_s - M^T_s)],
\end{equation*}
so $M - M^T$ is $\P_{12}$-martingale relative to
$\{\sF_t\}_{t\geq 0}$.$\endproof$

\bl\label{L3.15}
Let $\P$ be a probability measure on $(\OmegaEd,\sFEd)$,
and let $M$ be a uniformly integrable $\P$-martingale
relative to $\{\sFEd_t\}_{t\geq 0}$.  Let $S$, $T$ and $U$
be stopping times with $T\leq U$ almost surely, and let
$Z$ be an $\sFEd_T$-measurable bounded random variable.  Then
$\E\big[(M_U-M_T)Z\,\big|\,\sFEd_S\big]
=(M_{U\wedge S}-M_{T\wedge S})Z$.
\el

\noi
{\sc Proof:}
Because
$$
\ind_{\{S\leq T\}}\E\big[(M_U-M_T)Z\,\big|\,\sFEd_S\big]
=\ind_{\{S\leq T\}}\E\Big[Z\E\big[(M_U-M_T)\,\big|\,\sFEd_T\big]
\,\Big|\,\sFEd_S\Big]
=0,
$$
we have
\beas
\hspace{0.75in}
\lefteqn{\E\big[(M_U-M_T)Z\,\big|\,\sFEd_S\big]}\\
&=&
\ind_{\{T<S\leq U\}}\E\big[(M_U-M_T)Z\,\big|\,\sFEd_S\big]
+\ind_{\{U<S\}}\E\big[(M_U-M_T)Z\,\big|\,\sFEd_S\big]\\
&=&
\ind_{\{T<S\leq U\}}(M_S-M_T)Z
+\ind_{\{U<S\}}(M_U-M_T)Z\\
&=&
(M_{U\wedge S}-M_{T\wedge S})Z.
\hspace{3.15in}\endproof
\eeas

\bl\label{L3.16}
Let $\P_1$ and $\P_2$
be probability measures on $(\OmegaEd,\sFEd)$
and let $T$ be a finite (for every $\omega$)
\gbmarginpar{Added hypen before stopping time and
  $\{\sFEd_t\}_{t\geq 0}$- before adapted.
$\{\sFEd_t\}_{t\geq 0}$-stopping time.
Let $M^1$, $M^2$ and $C$ be continuous
$\{\sFEd_t\}_{t\geq 0}$-adapted real-valued processes
such that $M^1$, $M^2$ and $M^3\define M^1M^2-C$ are local
martingales relative to $\{\sFEd_t\}_{t\geq 0}$ under $\P_1$ and $\P_2$.
Let $\sG$ be a sub-$\sigma$-field of $\sFEd_T$ such that
$\P_1|_{\sG}\ll\P_2|_{\sG}$ and assume that
$\Mhat^1\define\Delta(M^1,T)$,
$\Mhat^2\define\Delta(M^2,T)$ and $\Chat\define\Delta(C,T)$
are $\sG\vee\sigma(\Delta(X,T))$-measurable.
Then $(M^3,\sFEd_t)_{t\geq 0}$ is a
local martingale under $\P_{12}\define\P_1\otimes_{\sG,T}\P_2$.
\el

\noi
{\sc Proof:}
We cannot apply Lemma \ref{L3.14} directly because we
did not assume that
$\Mhat_3$ is $\sG\vee\sigma(\Delta(X,T))$-measurable.
Instead, we define the process
\beas
Y_t
&\define&
M_{t\wedge T}^1M_{t\wedge T}^2
+(M_t^1-M_{t\wedge T}^1)(M_t^2-M_{t\wedge T}^2)-C_t\\
&=&
M_t^3-(M_t^1-M_{t\wedge T}^1)M_{t\wedge T}^2
-(M_t^2-M_{t\wedge T}^2)M_{t\wedge T}^1,\quad t\geq 0,
\eeas
for which $\Delta(Y,T)=\Delta(M^1,T)\Delta(M^2,T)-\Delta(C,T)$ is
$\sG\vee\sigma(\Delta(X,T))$-measurable.
Define
$T_n\define
\inf\big\{t\geq 0:|M_t^1|\vee|M_t^2|\vee|M_t^3|
\vee|C_t|\geq n\big\}$,
and set $M^{i,n}\define (M^i)^{T_n}$ for $i=1,2,3$,
$C^n\define C^{T_n}$ and $Y^n\define Y^{T_n}$.  For fixed $n$,
the processes $M^{i,n}$, $i=1,2,3$, and $Y^n$ are bounded.
For $0\leq s\leq t$,
we apply Lemma \ref{L3.15} with $M=M^{1,n}$, $Z=M_{t\wedge T}^{2,n}$,
$S=s$, $T=t\wedge T$ and $U=t$, and use the fact that
$M_s^{1,n}-M_{s\wedge T}^{1,n}=0$ if $T\geq s$ to obtain
\bea
\E_k\big[(M_t^{1,n}-M_{t\wedge T}^{1,n})M_{t\wedge T}^{2,n}
\,\big|\,\sFEd_s\big]
&=&
(M_s^{1,n}-M_{s\wedge T}^{1,n})M_{t\wedge T}^{2,n}\nonumber\\
&=&
(M_s^{1,n}-M_{s\wedge T}^{1,n})M_{s\wedge T}^{2,n},
\quad k=1,2.\quad\quad\label{3.24}
\eea
The same equality holds if we reverse the roles of $M^{1,n}$
and $M^{2,n}$.  Finally, because $M^{3,n}$ is a martingale,
\beas
\E_k[Y_t^n\,|\,\sFEd_s]
&=&
\E_k[M_t^{3,n}\,|\,\sFEd_s]
-\E_k\big[(M_t^{1,n}-M_{t\wedge T}^{1,n})M_{t\wedge T}^{2,n}
\,\big|\,\sFEd_s\big]\\
&&\qquad
-\E_k\big[(M_t^{2,n}-M_{t\wedge T}^{2,n}\big)M_{t\wedge T}^{1,n}
\,\big|\,\sFEd_s\big]\\
&=&
M_s^{3,n}-(M_s^{1,n}-M_{s\wedge T}^{1,n})M_{s\wedge T}^{2,n}
-(M_s^{2,n}-M_{s\wedge T}^{2,n})M_{s\wedge T}^{1,n}\\
&=&
Y_s^n,\quad k=1,2,
\eeas
so $Y$ is a local martingale under both $\P_1$ and $\P_2$.
Lemma \ref{L3.14} implies that $M^1$, $M^2$ and $Y$
are $\P_{12}$-local martingales.  Therefore, (\ref{3.24})
holds under $\P_{12}$ as well,
from which we conclude that
\beas
\hspace{0.4in}\E_{12}[M_t^{3,n}\,|\,\sFEd_s]
&=&
\E_{12}[Y_t^n\,|\,\sFEd_s]
+\E_{12}\big[(M_t^{1,n}-M_{t\wedge T}^{1,n})M_{t\wedge T}^{2,n}
\,\big|\,\sFEd_s\big]\\
&&\qquad
+\E_{12}\big[(M_t^{2,n}-M_{t\wedge T}^{2,n})M_{t\wedge T}^{1,n}
\,\big|\,\sFEd_s\big]\\
&=&
Y_s^n+(M_s^{1,n}-M_{s\wedge T}^{1,n})M_{s\wedge T}^{2,n}
+(M_s^{2,n}-M_{s\wedge T}^{2,n})M_{s\wedge T}^{1,n}\\
&=&
M_s^{3,n},\quad 0\leq s\leq t.
\hspace{2.30in}\endproof
\eeas

\noi
{\sc Proof of Proposition \ref{P3.12}:}
According to Remark \ref{R3.8}, $\P^{\otimes\Pi}=\P^{n+1}$,
where $\P^i$ is defined
recursively by $\P^0=\P$ and
$\P^{i+1}=\P^i\otimes_{T_i,\sG_i}\P$, $i=0,\dots,n$.
If $M$ is a continuous local martingale under $\P$
and $\Delta(M,T_i)$ is
$\sG_i\vee\sigma(\Delta(X,T_i))$-measurable
for $i=0,\dots,n$, then
repeated application of Lemma \ref{L3.14} shows that
$M$ is a $\P^i$-local martingale for
$i=1,\dots,n,n+1$, and in particular,
$M$ is a continuous local martingale
under $\P^{\otimes\Pi}$.  Similarly, if $M^1$ and $M^2$
are continuous local martingales under $\P$,
$C$ is a finite variation process such that
$M^3\define M^1M^2-C$ is a local martingale under $\P$,
and $\Delta(M^1,T_i)$, $\Delta(M^2,T_i)$ and $\Delta(C,T_i)$
are $\sG_i\vee\sigma(\Delta(X,T_i))$-measurable for $0=1,\dots,n$,
then repeated application of Lemma \ref{L3.16} shows
that $M^1M^2-C$ is a $\P^i$-local
martingale for $i=1,\dots,n,n+1$.
In particular, $M^1M^2-C$ is a continuous local martingale
under $\P^{\otimes\Pi}$.
These observations combined
with Proposition \ref{P3.9}(a)
prove the desired result. $\endproof$

\section{Conditional Expectations}
\label{SecCondExp}
\setcounter{equation}{1}

The results of this section are implicit in
Krylov \cite{Kry3} and Gy\"ongy \cite{G}.
We use the notation introduced in Sections
\ref{SecMainResult} and \ref{SConMea}.  In addition,
we denote the Borel $\sigma$-field on $[0,t]$
by $\sB[0,t]$ and the Borel $\sigma$-field on
$[0,\infty)$ by $\sB[0,\infty)$.

\bp\label{P4.1}
Let $Z$ be an $\sE$-valued process and let
$\Gamma$ be an $\R^d$-valued process
(respectively, a $d\times d$ matrix-valued process) taking
values in a closed convex set $K$, and satisfying
$\E[\int_0^t\|\Gamma_u\|\,du]
<\infty$ for all $t\geq 0$.
Then there
exists a nonrandom $\R^d$-valued measurable
function (respectively, a nonrandom $d\times d$ matrix-valued
measurable function) $\Gammahat$, defined on
$[0,\infty)\times\sE$, taking values in $K$,
and there exists a Lebesgue-null set $N\subset[0,\infty)$,
so that
\be\label{4.2}
\Gammahat(t,Z_t)=\E[\Gamma_t\,|\,Z_t],\quad  t\in N^c.
\ee
\ep

The proof of Proposition \ref{P4.1} depends on the following
lemma.

\bl\label{L4.2}
Let $Z$ be an $\sE$-valued process and let
$\Gamma$ be a real-valued process satisfying
$\E\int_0^t|\Gamma_u|\,du<\infty$ for all $t\geq 0$.
Let $\Gammahat$ be a nonrandom real-valued measurable function
on $[0,\infty)\times\sE$.  There exists a
Lebesgue-null set $N\subset[0,\infty)$ so that (\ref{4.2})
holds if and only if for every bounded
$\sB[0,\infty)\otimes\frakE$-measurable real-valued
function $f$,
\be\label{4.4}
\E\int_0^t\Gammahat(u,Z_u)f(u,Z_u)\,du
=\E\int_0^t\Gamma_uf(u,Z_u)\,du,\quad t\geq 0.
\ee
\el

\noi
{\sc Proof:}  If (\ref{4.2}) holds, then (\ref{4.4}) follows
from Fubini's Theorem.

To prove the converse, we assume (\ref{4.4}).
Taking $f(u,Z_u)=\mbox{sgn}(\Gammahat(u,Z_u))$
and using the integrability of $\Gamma$, we
see that $\E\int_0^t|\Gammahat(u,Z_u)|\,du<\infty$
for all $t\geq 0$.

The $\sigma$-field $\frakE$ is generated by
a collection of open balls intersected
with $\sE$, each ball having a rational radius and centered
at a point in a countable dense subset of the
separable metric space containing $\sE$.  Let $\sO$
denote the collection of finite intersections of
this countable collection of sets.  Then $\sO$
is itself countable and $\frakE=\sigma(\sO)$.
We enumerate the sets in $\sO$ as
$O_1,O_2,\dots$.
Define
$g_n(t)\define
\E\big[\big(\Gammahat(t,Z_t)-\Gamma_t\big)
\ind_{\{Z_t\in O_n\}}\big]$.
For $B\in\sB[0,t]$, (\ref{4.4}) implies
$$
\int_Bg_n(u)\,du=
\E\int_0^t\big(\Gammahat(u,Z_u)-\Gamma_u\big)
\ind_{\{(u,Z_u)\in B\times O_n\}}\,du=0.
$$
Since both $t\geq 0$ and $B\in\sB[0,t]$ are arbitrary,
we conclude that $g_n=0$ for Lebesgue-almost every $t\geq 0$.
Thus,
$N\define\{t\geq 0|g_n(t)\neq 0\mbox{ for some }n\}$
is a Lebesgue-null set.
The collection of sets $A\in\frakE$ for which
\be\label{4.5}
\E[(\Gammahat(t,Z_t)-\Gamma_t)\ind_{\{Z_t\in A\}}]=0,
\quad t\in N^c
\ee
is a $\lambda$ system containing $\sO$,
and the Dynkin $\pi$-$\lambda$
theorem implies that (\ref{4.5}) holds for
every $A\in\frakE$.  This gives us (\ref{4.2}).
$\endproof$

\vspace{\baselineskip}
\noi
{\sc Proof of Proposition \ref{P4.1}:}
Except for the assertion that $\Gammahat$ takes values
in the set $K$, it suffices to prove
the proposition for the case that $\Gamma$
is real-valued.  We can then apply the one-dimensional
result to each
component of the $\Gamma$ in the proposition.

In the one-dimensional case, we define the $\sigma$-finite
measure
$$
\mu(A)\define\E\int_0^{\infty}\ind_A(u,Z_u)\,du,
\quad A\in\sB[0,\infty)\otimes\frakE,
$$
and the $\sigma$-finite signed measure
$$
\nu(A)\define\E\int_0^{\infty}\Gamma_u\ind_A(u,Z_u)\,du,
\quad A\in\sB[0,\infty)\otimes\frakE.
$$
Obviously, $\nu\ll\mu$, so we can define
$\Gammahat(t,z)=\frac{d\nu}{d\mu}(t,z)$ for
$(t,z)\in[0,\infty]\otimes\sE$.
Let $f$ be a bounded $\sB[0,\infty)\otimes\frakE$-measurable
real-valued function.  For $t\geq 0$,
\beas
\E\int_0^t\Gammahat(u,Z_u)f(u,Z_u)\,du
&=&
\int_{[0,t]\times\sE}
\Gammahat(u,z)f(u,z)\mu(du,dz)\\
&=&
\int_{[0,t]\times\sE}
f(u,z)\,\nu(du,dz)\\
&=&
\E\int_0^t\Gamma_uf(u,Z_u)\,du.
\eeas
Equation (\ref{4.2}) follows from Lemma \ref{L4.2}.

Let us now consider the case of a multi-dimensional $\Gamma$
taking values in a closed convex set $K$.
We have already shown the existence of $\Gammahat$ such
that (\ref{4.2}) holds, and it remains to show
that $\Gammahat$ takes values in $K$.
Define $\varphi\colon\R^d\rightarrow\R$
(respectively, $\varphi\colon\R^d\times\R^d\rightarrow\R$) by
$\varphi(\gamma)=\min_{\kappa\in K}\|\gamma-\kappa\|$,
which is the distance from $\gamma$ to $K$.  One can verify
from the triangle inequality that for each constant $c$,
the set $\{\gamma|\varphi(\gamma)\leq c\}$ is convex,
and hence $\varphi$ is a continuous convex real-valued function.
Such a function has the property that
$\varphi(\gamma)=\max\{\ell(\gamma)|
\ell\mbox{ is linear and }\ell\leq\varphi\}$.
This permits us to establish the Jensen inequality
\beas
\E\big[\varphi(\Gamma_t)\,\big|\,Z_t\big]
&\geq&
\max\Big\{\E\big[\ell(\Gamma_t)\,\big|\,Z_t\big]\,\Big|\,
\ell\mbox{ is linear and }\ell\leq\varphi\Big\}\\
&=&
\max\Big\{\ell\big(\E[\Gamma_t\,|\,Z_t]\big)\,\Big|\,
\ell\mbox{ is linear and }\ell\leq\varphi\Big\}\\
&=&
\varphi\big(\E[\Gamma_t\,|\,Z_t]\big)\\
&=&
\varphi\big(\Gammahat(t,Z_t)\big), \quad t\in N^c.
\eeas
But $\Gamma$ takes values in $K$,
so the left-hand side of this inequality is zero.
Thus the right-hand side is zero,
implying $\Gammahat(t,Z_t)\in K$ almost surely
for each $t\in N^c$.
We can modify $\Gammahat(t,z)$
so that it takes values in $K$ for every
$t$, and (\ref{4.2}) still holds. $\endproof$

\begin{definition}\label{D4.3}
Let $\{\Gamma^i\}_i$ be a collection of processes on
some probability space $(\Omega,\sF,\P)$
and let $T$ be a $[0,\infty)$-valued random
variable.  We say the collection $\{\Gamma^i\}_i$
is {\em strongly independent} of
$T$ if there is a $\sigma$-field $\sG\subset\sF$
such that each $\Gamma_i$ is $\sB[0,\infty)\times\sG$-measurable
and $\sG$ is independent of $\sigma(T)$.
\end{definition}

\bp\label{P4.5}
Within the setting of Proposition \ref{P4.1},
let $T$ be a $[0,\infty)$-valued random variable
whose distribution $\mu\define \P\circ T^{-1}$
is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue
measure.  Assume also that the pair
of processes $(\Gamma, Z)$ is strongly
independent of $T$ and $\E|\Gamma_T|<\infty$.  Then
\be\label{4.7}
\Gammahat(T,Z_T)=\E[\Gamma_T\,|\,T,Z_T].
\ee
\ep

\noi
{\bf Proof:}
We first observe that
\be\label{4.6}
\int_0^{\infty}\E[\Xi_t]\,\mu(dt)
=\E[\Xi_T]
\ee
for any process $\Xi$ that is strongly independent
of $T$ and
satisfies $\E|\Xi_T|<\infty$.
To see this, consider the case
$\Xi_t=\sum_{i=1}^n\ind_{A_i}\ind_{B_i}(t)$,
where $A_i\in\sG$, the $\sigma$-field
in Definition \ref{D4.3}, and $B_i\in\sB[0,\infty)$.
Then use the monotone class theorem.

Now let $f\colon[0,\infty)\times\sE\rightarrow\R$
be a bounded, $\sB[0,\infty)\otimes\frakE$-measurable
real-valued function.  Proposition \ref{P4.1}
implies
$\E\big[\Gammahat(t,Z_t)f(t,Z_t)\big]
=\E\big[\Gamma_tf(t,Z_t)\big]$ for all $t\in N^c$.
Integrating both sides of this equation
with respect to $\mu(dt)$
and using (\ref{4.6}), we obtain
$\E\big[\Gammahat(T,Z_T)f(T,Z_T)\big]
=\E\big[\Gamma_Tf(T,Z_T)\big]$.
Equation (\ref{4.7}) follows. $\endproof$

\section{Approximation}\label{S5}

We collect in this section three approximation results needed to prove
Theorem \ref{T2.4}.  We denote by $\N$ the set of natural numbers and
define $\Nbar\define\N\cup\{\infty\}$.  We recall that
$\lambda_{[0,t]}$
denotes Lebesgue measure on $[0,t]$.


\subsection{Convergence of the integral
of a process}\label{S5.1}

\bp\label{P5.2}
Let $\{Z^m\}_{m\in\Nbar}$ be a collection
of continuous $\sE$-valued processes,
possibly defined on different probability
spaces under different probability
measures $\Q^m$.
Let
$f\colon[0,\infty)\times\sE\rightarrow \R^d$
be a measurable function.  Assume
\ben
\item[(i)]
for each $t\in[0,\infty)$,
the distribution of $Z_t^m$ under $\Q^m$ is independent of
$m\in\N$,
\item[(ii)]
the distribution on $C^{\sE}$
of $Z^m$ under $\Q^m$ converges weakly to the distribution
of $Z^{\infty}$ under $\Q^{\infty}$, i.e.,
$\Q^m\circ(Z^m)^{-1}\Rightarrow\Q^{\infty}\circ(Z^{\infty})^{-1}$,
and
\item[(iii)]
$\E^{\Q^1}\int_0^t\|f(u,Z_u^1)\|\,du
<\infty$ for every $t\in[0,\infty)$.
\een
Then
\ben
\item[(iv)]
for every $m\in\Nbar$ the
integral process
$F_t^m\define\int_0^tf(s,Z_s^m)\,ds$,
$t\in[0,\infty)$,
is defined $\Q^m$-almost surely,
\item[(v)]
$\Q^m[F^m\in C^d]=1$ for every
$m\in\Nbar$,
\item[(vi)]
$\{f(\cdot,Z^m_{\cdot}),\lambda_{[0,t]}\times\Q^m
\}_{m\in\Nbar}$ is uniformly integrable
for every $t\in[0,\infty)$,
\item[(v)]
$(Z^m,F^m)\Rightarrow (Z^{\infty},F^{\infty})$.
\een
\ep

\noi
{\sc Proof:}
It suffices to prove parts (iv)--(vi)
of the lemma for
the case $d=1$, since these results
can be applied component-wise
to the $d$-dimensional $f$.

Define the measure
$\mu$ on $[0,\infty)\times\sE$ by
$\mu(A)\define\E^{\Q^m}
\int_0^{\infty}\ind_A(s,Z^m_s)\,ds$.
Assumption (i) and
the convergence in (ii) imply that
the distribution of $Z^m_t$
is independent of
$m\in\Nbar$, so it does not matter
which $m\in\Nbar$ we use in the definition
of $\mu$.  Therefore, for each
$m\in\Nbar$ and $M>0$,
\beas
\E^{\Q^m}\int_0^t|f(s,Z^m_s)|
\ind_{\{|f(x,Z^m_s)|\geq M\}}\,ds
&=&
\int_{[0,t]\times\sE}
|f(s,e)|\ind_{\{|f(s,e)|\geq M\}}
\mu(ds,de)\\
&=&
\E^{\Q^1}\int_0^t|f(s,Z_s^1)|
\ind_{\{|f(s,Z_s^1)|\geq M\}}\,ds.
\eeas
Setting $M=0$, we obtain (iv) and (v) from (iii).
Condition (iii) implies that the
last term can be made arbitrarily
small by choosing $M$ large,
and (vi) also follows.

To prove (v), we use (vi) and
Lusin's Theorem
to choose for each $k\in\N$ a bounded
continuous function
$f^k\colon[0,k]\times\sE\rightarrow\R^d$ such
that
$$
\lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}
\int_{[0,k]\times\sE}
\|f(t,e)-f^k(t,e)\|\,\mu(dt,de)=0.
$$
The mapping
$z\mapsto\int_0^{\cdot\wedge k}f^k(s,z(s))ds$
is continuous from $C^{\sE}$ to
$C^d$, which implies that
\be\label{5.8}
(Z^m,F^{m,k})\Rightarrow
(Z^{\infty},F^{\infty,k})\mbox{ as }m\rightarrow\infty,
\ee
where
$F^{m,k}_t\define
\int_0^{t\wedge k}f^k(s,Z_s^m)ds$.
But for each fixed $T$ and $k\geq T$,
\bea
\sup_{m\in\Nbar}
\Q^m\left[\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}
\|F_t^m-F_t^{m,k}\|>\epsilon\right]
&\leq&
\sup_{m\in\Nbar}
\frac{1}{\epsilon} \,
\E^{\Q^m} \hskip -0.75em \sup_{0\leq t\leq T}
\|F^m_t-F^{m,k}_t\|\nonumber\\
&\leq&
\frac{1}{\epsilon}
\int_{[0,k]\times\sE}
\|f(s,e)-f^k(s,e)\|\,\mu(ds,de),\quad
\label{5.8a}
\eea
which has limit zero as $k\rightarrow\infty$.
In particular, the convergence
$F^{m,k}\Rightarrow F^m$ as
$k\rightarrow\infty$ is uniform
in $m\in\Nbar$.

Let $\Psi\colon C^{\sE}\times C^1\rightarrow
\R$ be a uniformly continuous bounded function.
To prove weak convergence of measures on a metric space,
it suffices to consider such functions; see \cite{P},
Chapter II, Theorem 6.1.
We have
\beas
\lefteqn{\Big|\E^m\big[\Psi(Z^m,F^m)]
-\E^\infty[\Psi(Z^{\infty},F^{\infty})\big]\Big|}\\
&=&
\Big|\E^m\big[\Psi(Z^m\!,F^m)
-\Psi(Z^m\!,F^{m,k})\big]\Big|
+\Big|\E^m\big[\Psi(Z^m\!,F^{m,k})]
-\E^\infty[\Psi(Z^{\infty}\!,F^{\infty,k})
\big]\Big|\\
&&\qquad
+\Big|\E^\infty\big[\Psi(Z^{\infty},F^{\infty,k})
-\Psi(Z^{\infty},F^{\infty})\big]\Big|.
\eeas
Given $\epsilon>0$, (\ref{5.8a}) guarantees that
we can choose $k$ so large that
the first and third
terms on the right hand side
are less than  $\epsilon$, independently
of $m$.  For this value of $k$, we can then use (\ref{5.8})
to choose $M$ so that for all $m\geq M$, the second
term is also less than $\epsilon$.
$\endproof$

\subsection{Approximation by step functions}
\label{S5.2}

We show in Proposition \ref{P5.5} below
that an arbitrary integrable process
can be approximated in $L_1(\P\times\lambda_{[0,t]})$
by step functions obtained by sampling
the process at random partition points.


\bl\label{L5.4}
Let $f\colon[0,\infty)\rightarrow\R^d$
be a measurable function with
$\int_0^t\|f(s)\|ds<\infty$
for every $t\in[0,\infty)$.
Define the sets
\be\label{5.9a}
I_i^n\define\left\{(t,u)\in[0,\infty)\times[0,1]:
\frac{u+i-1}{n}\leq t<\frac{u+i}{n}\right\},\quad
i=1,2,\dots,
\ee
and define the sequence of
functions
$f_n(t,u)=\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}
f\left(\frac{u+i-1}{n}\right)
\ind_{I_i^n}(t,u)$.
Then
$$
\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}
\int_0^1\int_0^t
\|f(s)-f_n(s,u)\|\,ds\,du=0,
\quad t\in[0,\infty).
$$
\el

\noi
{\sc Proof:}
Fix $t>0$ and $\epsilon>0$.
Choose a continuous, $\R^d$-valued
function $g$ defined on $[0,t+1]$
for which
$\int_0^{t+1}\|f(s)-g(s)\|ds\leq\epsilon$.
Set $m=\lceil t \rceil\in[t,t+1)\cap\N$
and set
\gbmarginpar{Moved definition of $g_n$ inline
  so that the next display fits on this page.
$
g_n(s,u)\define\sum_{i=1}^{mn}
g\left(\frac{u+i-1}{n}\right)
\ind_{I_i^n}(s,u).
$
We have
\beas
\lefteqn{
\int_0^1\int_0^t\|f_n(s,u)-g_n(s,u)\|\,ds\,du}\\
&\leq&
\sum_{i=1}^{mn}\int_0^1
\int_{\frac{u+i-1}{n}}^{\frac{u+i}{n}}
\left\|f\left(\frac{u+i-1}{n}\right)
-g\left(\frac{u+i-1}{n}\right)\right\|\,ds\,du\\
&=&
\sum_{i=1}^{mn}\int_0^1\left\|f\left(\frac{u+i-1}{n}\right)
-g\left(\frac{u+i-1}{n}\right)\right\|\frac{du}{n}\\
&=&
\sum_{i=1}^{mn}\int_{\frac{i-1}{n}}^{\frac{i}{n}}
\|f(v)-g(v)\|\,dv
\,\,\leq\,\,
\epsilon.
\eeas
Because $g$ is uniformly continuous on $[0,t+1]$,
we may choose $N$ so that $\|g(s_2)-g(s_1)\|\leq \epsilon/t$
whenever $|s_2-s_1|\leq 1/N$.  By enlarging $N$
if necessary, we can also ensure that
$\int_0^{1/N}\|g(s)\|ds\leq\epsilon$.
Therefore, for $n\geq N$, we have
\beas
\hspace{0.45in}
\lefteqn{\int_0^1\int_0^t\|f(s)-f_n(s,u)\|\,ds\,du}\\
&\leq&
\int_0^t\|f(s)-g(s)\|\,ds
+\int_0^1\int_{u/n}^t\|g(s)-g_n(s,u)\|\,ds\,du\\
&&\qquad
+\int_0^{1/n}\|g(s)\|\,ds
+\int_0^1\int_0^t\|g_n(s,u)-f_n(s,u)\|\,ds\,du
\,\,\leq\,\,
4\epsilon.
\hspace{0.6in}\,\,\,
\endproof
\eeas

\bp\label{P5.5}
Let $(\Omega',\sF',\Q')$ be a probability space that
supports an $\R^d$-valued process $a$ satisfying
\be\label{5.10}
\E^{\Q'}\int_0^t\|a_s\|\,ds<\infty,
\quad t\geq0.
\ee
Set $\Omega\define[0,1]\times\Omega'$, with generic
point $\omega=(u,\omega')$, and define
$U(u,\omega')=u$.  Set $\sF=\sB[0,1]\otimes\sF'$,
$\Q=\lambda_{[0,1]}\times\Q'$, and extend $a$ to
$\Omega$ via the abuse of notation
$a(u,\omega')\define a(\omega')$.
Finally, define the random times $T_0^n\define 0$,
$T_i^n\define(U+i-1)/n$ for $i=1,2,\dots,n^2$,
and $T_{n^2+1}^n\define\infty$.  Then the
{\em sampled process}
$$
a^n_t(\omega)
\define
\sum_{i=1}^{n^2}a_{T_i^n(\omega)}(\omega)
\ind_{[T_i^n(\omega),T_i^{n+1}(\omega))}(t)=
\sum_{i=1}^{n^2}a_{(u+i-1)/n}(\omega')
\ind_{I_i^n}(t,u),
$$
where
$I_i^n$ is defined by (\ref{5.9a}),
satisfies
\be\label{5.11}
\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\E^{\Q}\int_0^t
\|a_s-a_s^n\|\,ds=0,\quad t\geq 0.
\ee
\ep

\noi
{\sc Proof:}
Define
$A^n_t(\omega')\define\int_0^1\int_0^t
\|a_s(\omega')-a_s^n(u,\omega')\|\,ds\,du$ for $t\geq 0$
and $\omega'\in\Omega'$.
Assumption (\ref{5.10}) implies that
$\int_0^t\|a_s(\omega')\|\,ds<\infty$ for all
$t\geq 0$ for $\Q'$-almost every
$\omega'$.  For fixed $\omega'$ satisfying this condition,
Lemma \ref{L5.4} then shows that
$\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}A_t^n(\omega')=0$ for every $t\geq 0$.
Equation (\ref{5.11}) is equivalent to
$$
\lim_{n\rightarrow 0}\E^{\Q'}A_t^n=0,\quad t\geq 0,
$$
and to obtain this result it now suffices to show that
for each fixed $t\geq 0$, the collection of random variables
$\{A_t^n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ is uniformly integrable under $\Q'$.

We first show that $\{a^n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ is uniformly
integrable with respect
to $\lambda_{[0,t]}\times\Q$ for every $t\geq 0$.
Toward this end, fix $t\geq 0$ and set $m\define\lceil t\rceil
\in[t,t+1)\cap\N$, so that $t\leq T_{mn+1}^n$.
\gbmarginpar{I broke a single display into two pieces so that
  the first piece could fit on this page.
Then
\beas
\E^{\Q}\left[\|a_{T_i^n}\|\ind_{\{\|a_{T_i^n}\|\geq M\}}\right]
&=&
\int_0^1\E^{\Q'}\left[\|a_{(u+i-1)/n}^n\|
\ind_{\{\|a_{(u+i-1)/n}\|\geq M\}}\right]\,\frac{du}{n}\\
&=&
\int_{(i-1)/n}^{i/n}
\E^{\Q'}\left[\|a_s\|\ind_{\{\|a_s\|\geq M\}}\right]\,ds,
\qquad i=1, \dots, mn,\\
\eeas
and
\beas
\E^{\Q}\int_0^t\|a_s^n\|\ind_{\{\|a_s^n\|\geq M\}}\,ds
&\leq&
\E^{\Q}\int_0^{T_{mn+1}^n}\|a_s^n\|\ind_{\{\|a_s^n\|\geq M\}}\,ds\\
&=&
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{mn}
\E^{\Q}\left[\|a_{T_i^n}\|\ind_{\{\|a_{T_i^n}\|\geq M\}}\right]\\
&=&
\E^{\Q'}\int_0^m\|a_s\|\ind_{\{\|a_s\|\geq M\}}\,ds.
\eeas
The uniform integrability of $\{a^n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ under
$\lambda_{[0,t]}\times\Q$ follows from (\ref{5.10}).
This implies the uniform
integrability of $\{\|a-a^n\|\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$.
Jensen's inequality implies
\beas
\E^{\Q'}\left[(A_t^n-M)^+\right]
&=&
\E^{\Q'}\left[\left(\int_0^1\int_0^t
\|a_s(\cdot)-a_s^n(u,\cdot)\|\,ds\,du-M\right)^+\right]\\
&\leq&
\E^{\Q'}\left[\int_0^1\left(\int_0^t
\|a_s(\cdot)-a_s^n(u,\cdot)\|\,ds-M\right)^+du\right]\\
&=&
\E^{\Q}\left[\left(\int_0^t\|a_s-a_s^n\|\,ds-M\right)^+\right]\\
&\leq&
\E^{\Q}\left[\int_0^t\left(\|a_s-a_s^n\|
-\frac{M}{t}\right)^+\,ds\right],
\eeas
and the uniform integrability of $\{\|a-a^n\|\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ under
$\lambda_{[0,t]}\times\Q$ implies
that for every $\epsilon>0$, there exists $M_{\epsilon}>0$ such that
$$
\sup_{n\in\N}\E^{\Q'}\left[(A_t^n-M_{\epsilon})^+\right]\leq\epsilon.
$$
Consequently,
\beas
\sup_{n\in\N}\E^{\Q'}
\big[A_t^n\ind_{\{A_t^n\geq 2M_{\epsilon}\}}\big]
&=&
\sup_{n\in\N}
\E^{\Q'}\big[(A_t^n-2M_{\epsilon})^+
+2M_{\epsilon}\ind_{\{A_t^n\geq 2M_{\epsilon}\}}\big]\\
&\leq&
\sup_{n\in\N}
\E^{\Q'}\big[(A_t^n-2M_{\epsilon})^+
+2(A_t^n-M_{\epsilon})^+\big]\\
&\leq&
3\sup_{n\in\N}
\E^{Q'}\big[(A_t^n-M_{\epsilon})^+\big]\\
&\leq&
 3\epsilon.
\eeas
This proves the uniform
integrability of $\{A_t^n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$
under $\Q'$. $\endproof$

\subsection{Sequence of discrete-time
martingales with zero limit}\label{S5.3}
For our final approximation result, we construct a sequence of
continuous-time, finite-variation processes that are
martingales when sampled at certain discrete times.
We provide conditions under which this sequence
must converge to zero.

\begin{definition}\label{D5.6}
A {\em random partition} $\Pi$ is a set of random times
$0=T_0\leq T_1\leq\dots\leq T_n$.  We set
$|\Pi|(\omega)\define\sup_{1\leq i\leq n}|T_i(\omega)-T_{i-1}(\omega)|$.
Let $\{\Pi^m\}_{m=1}^{\infty}$ be a sequence of random partitions,
possibly defined on different spaces $\{\Omega^m\}_{m=1}^{\infty}$,
where the random times in the partitions $\Pi^m$ are denoted
$T_0^m\leq T_1^m\leq\dots\leq T_{N(m)}^m$.  We say that
$\{\Pi^m\}_{m=1}^{\infty}$ {\em converges uniformly
to the identity} if
\be\label{5.13a}
\lim_{m\rightarrow\infty}\sup_{\omega\in\Omega^m}
|\Pi^m(\omega)|=0\mbox{ and }
\lim_{m\rightarrow\infty}\inf_{\omega\in\Omega^m}
T_{N(m)}^m(\omega)=\infty.
\ee
\end{definition}

\bp\label{P5.7}
Let $(\Omega^m,\sF^m,\P^m)_{m=1}^{\infty}$ be a sequence of probability
spaces.  Assume that on each space there is defined an
$\R^d$-valued process $X^m$
and a random partition
$\Pi^m=\{T_0^m,T_1^m,\dots T_{N(m)}^m\}$,
and these partitions converge uniformly to the identity.
Assume further that the set of processes and measures
$(X^m,\lambda_{[0,t]}\times\P^m)_{m=1}^{\infty}$
is uniformly
integrable for every $t\geq 0$.
For $k=0,1,\dots,N(m)$, define
$Y_k^m\define\int_0^{T_k^m}X_u^m\,du$ and
$\sF_k^m\define\sigma(Y_j^m,T_j^m\,|\,0\leq j\leq k)$,
and assume that $(Y_k^m,\sF_k^m)_{0\leq k\leq N(m)}$ is
a martingale for each $m$.  Then
$$
\lim_{m\rightarrow\infty}\E^m
\sup_{0\leq s\leq t}\left\|\int_0^sX_u^m\,du\right\|
=0,\quad t\geq 0.
$$
\ep

\noi
{\sc Proof:}
By considering components of $\int_0^sX^m_udu$, we may reduce
the proof to the case $d=1$.  Fix $t\geq 0$.
Fix $m$ large enough that $\sup_{\omega\in\Omega^m}|\Pi^m|(\omega)\leq 1$
and $\inf_{\omega\in\Omega^m}T_{N(m)}^m(\omega)>t$.
Define  $\rho\define \min\{k:T_k^m\geq t\}$, so that
$T_{\rho}^m$ is the first random time
after $t$ and
$T_{\rho}^m\leq T_{N(m)}^m\wedge(t+1)$.  The discrete-time
martingale $Y^m$ stopped at $T_{\rho}^m$ is still a martingale.
For $0\leq s\leq t$, set
$\tau(s)\define\max\{k:T_k^m\leq s\}$,
so that $T_{\tau(s)}^m$ is the last random time before $s$.
Then $\tau(s)\leq\rho$ and $0\leq s-T_{\tau(s)}^m\leq|\Pi^m|$.
For $M>0$,
\beas
\left|\int_0^sX_u^m\,du\right|
&\leq&
|Y_{\tau(s)}^m|
+\int^s_{T_{\tau(s)}^m}|X^m_u|\,du \nonumber\\
&\leq&
|Y_{\tau(s)}^m|+\int_{T_{\tau(s)}^m}^s\big[\big(|X_u^m|-M\big)^++M\big]du\nonumber\\
&\leq&
\max_{1\leq k\leq \rho}|Y_k^m|
+\int_0^t\big(|X_u^m|-M\big)^+du+M|\Pi^m|.
\eeas
Maximizing over $s\in[0,t]$ and taking expectations, we obtain
\be\label{5.15}
\E^m\sup_{s\in[0,t]}\left|\int_0^sX_u^m\,du\right|
\leq
\E^m\max_{1\leq k\leq \rho}|Y_k^m|
+\E^m\int_0^t\big(|X_u^m|-M\big)^+du
+M\E^m|\Pi^m|.
\ee

We bound the first term on the right-hand side of (\ref{5.15}).
The discrete-time Burkholder-Davis-Gundy
inequality (e.g., \cite{Gar}, II.1.1) implies the existence of a
universal constant $C$ for which
\be\label{5.16}
\E^m\max_{1\leq k\leq \rho}|Y_k^m|
\leq
C\E^m\Bigg[\Bigg(\sum_{1\leq k\leq \rho}(Y_k^m-Y_{k-1}^m)^2
\Bigg)^{1/2}\Bigg].
\ee
The right-hand side of (\ref{5.16}) can be bounded
using H\"older's inequality.  In particular,
\bea
\lefteqn{
\E^m\Bigg[\Bigg(\sum_{1\leq k\leq \rho}(Y_k^m-Y_{k-1}^m)^2\Bigg)^{1/2}\Bigg]
}\nonumber\\
&\leq&
\E^m\Bigg[\max_{1\leq k\leq \rho}|Y_k^m-Y_{k-1}^m|^{1/2}
\cdot \Bigg(\sum_{1\leq k\leq \rho}|Y_k^m-Y_{k-1}^m|\Bigg)^{1/2}\Bigg]\nonumber\\
&\leq&
\E^m\Bigg[\max_{1\leq k\leq \rho}|Y_k^m-Y_{k-1}^m|^{1/2}
\cdot \Bigg(\int_0^{t+1}|X_u^m|\,du\Bigg)^{1/2}\Bigg]\nonumber\\
&\leq&
\sqrt{\E^m\max_{1\leq k\leq \rho}|Y_k^m-Y_{k-1}^m|}
\cdot
\sqrt{\E^m\int_0^{t+1}|X_u^m|\,du}\nonumber\\
&\leq&
\sqrt{\E^m\int_0^{t+1}\big(|X_u^m|-M\big)^+\,du+M\E^m|\Pi^m|}
\cdot
\sqrt{\E^m\int_0^{t+1}|X_u^m|\,du}.\qquad\label{5.17}
\eea
Combining (\ref{5.15})--(\ref{5.17}), we obtain
\beas
\lefteqn{\E^m\sup_{s\in[0,t]}
\left|\int_0^sX^m_u\,du\right|}\nonumber\\
&\leq &
C\sqrt{\E^m\int_0^{t+1}\big(|X_u^m|-M\big)^+\,du+M\E^m|\Pi^m|}
\cdot
\sqrt{\E^m\int_0^{t+1}|X_u^m|\,du}\nonumber\\
&&\quad
+\E^m\int_0^t\big(|X_u^m|-M\big)^+du
+M\E^m|\Pi|,\eeas
where $C$ does not depend on $X$ and $M\geq 0$ is arbitrary.
The uniform integrability of
$(X^m,\lambda_{[0,t+1]}\times\P^m)_{m=1}^{\infty}$ implies
that $\sup_{m}\E^m\int_0^{t+1}|X_u^m|du$ is a finite constant
$C'$.
Given $\epsilon>0$, uniform integrability further permits
us to choose $M$ so large that
$\sup_m\E^m\int_0^{t+1}(|X_u^m|-M)^+du\leq \epsilon$.  For such an $M$,
$$
\E^m\sup_{s\in[0,t]}\left|\int_0^sX^m_u\,du\right|
\leq C\sqrt{C'}\sqrt{\epsilon+ME^m|\Pi^m|}+\epsilon+M\E^m|\Pi^m|.
$$
Letting $m\rightarrow\infty$ and using the first part of (\ref{5.13a}),
we conclude that
$$
\hspace{1.35in}\limsup_{m\rightarrow\infty}
\E^m\sup_{s\in[0,t]}\left|\int_0^sX^m_u\,du\right|
\leq C\sqrt{C'\epsilon}+\epsilon.
\hspace{1.35in}\endproof
$$

\section{Proof of Theorem \ref{T2.4}}
\label{S6}
\setcounter{equation}{0}

We prove a theorem that is little
more than a restatement of Theorem \ref{T2.4} without
reference to the driving Brownian motions $W$ and $\What$
in that theorem.  We develop this connection immediately
after the statement of Theorem \ref{T6.1} below.
Recall Definition \ref{D3.11}.

\bt\label{T6.1} Let $\sE$ be a Polish space.  Let
$(\Omega,\sF,\{\sF_t\}_{t\geq 0},\P)$ be a
filtered probability space that supports an
$\sE$-valued random variable $Z_0$ and
an adapted continuous $\R^d$-valued semimartingale
$Y$ with $Y_0=0$ and with characteristic pair
$(B,C)$, where
\be\label{6.0}
B_t=\int_0^tb_s \, ds, \quad C_t=\int_0^tc_s \, ds,
\ee
and the adapted $\R^d$-valued
process $b$ and the adapted $\R^d\times\R^d$-valued
positive semidefinite process $c$
satisfy
\be\label{6.1}
\E\left[\int_0^t\big(\|b_s\|+\|c_s\|\big)\,ds\right]<\infty,
\quad t\geq 0.
\ee
Let $\bhat$ and $\chat$ be nonrandom measurable
functions defined on $[0,\infty)\times\sE$ with
$\bhat$ taking values in $\R^d$ and $\chat$ taking
values in the space of $d\times d$ positive
semidefinite matrices, and let $N\subset[0,\infty)$ be a
Lebesgue-null set such that
\be\label{6.2}
\bhat(t,Z_t)=
\E[b_t\,|\,Z_t],\quad
\chat(t,Z_t)=
\E[c_t\,|\,Z_t],\quad t\in N^c.
\ee
Define
$\OmegaEd\define\sE\times C_0^d$, let
$\Phi\colon\OmegaEd\rightarrow C^{\sE}$ be a continuous
updating function, and let $Z$ be the continuous,
$\sE$-valued process given by $Z=\Phi(Z_0,Y)$.
Let $\Yhat\colon\OmegaEd\rightarrow C_0^d$ be
given by $\Yhat(e,x)=x$ and
$\Zhat\colon\OmegaEd\rightarrow C^{\sE}$ be given
by $\Zhat = \Phi(e,x)$.  Then there exists a
measure $\Phat$ on $\OmegaEd$ such that
\begin{itemize}
\item[(i)]
$\Yhat$ is a semimartingale with
characteristic pair $(\Bhat,\Chat)$ under $\Phat$,
where $\Bhat_t\define\int_0^t\bhat(s,\Zhat_s)ds$ and
$\Chat_t\define\int_0^t\chat(s,\Zhat_s)ds$, and
\item[(ii)]
for each $t\geq 0$, the distribution of
$\Zhat_t$ under $\Phat$
agrees with the distribution of $Z_t$ under $\P$.
\end{itemize}
\et

\noi {\sc Proof of Theorem \ref{T2.4}:} Let us
assume Theorem \ref{T6.1}.  Then, under the
hypotheses of Theorem \ref{T2.4}, we may define
$c_s\define\sigma_s\sigma_s^{tr}$ and invoke
Proposition~\ref{P4.1} to ensure the existence of
nonrandom $\bhat$ and $\chat$ and a Lebesgue-null
set $N$ such that \eqref{6.2}
holds.  We then conclude that there exist $\Yhat$
and $\Zhat$ satisfying properties (i)--(ii) in
Theorem \ref{T6.1}.  To show that $\Yhat$ has the
representation (\ref{2.14}), we set $\sigmahat$
equal to the symmetric square root of $\chat$ and
invoke the It\^o integral representation (e.g.,
\cite{KS}, Chapter 3, Theorem 4.2) for the
$d$-dimensional local martingale
$\Yhat-\Bhat$. $\endproof$


\vspace{\baselineskip}
\noi
{\sc Proof of Theorem \ref{T6.1}:}
The proof, which involves a discretization, as suggested by
the example in Section \ref{DiscreteEx}, and then passage to the
limit, proceeds in several steps.

\vspace{\baselineskip}
\noi
\underline{Step 1: Construction of canonical space and processes}.

The random object of interest, $(Z_0,Y,B,C)$, takes values
in $\OmegaEd\times C_0^d\times C_0^{d^2}$.  In order to show that the
discretization has a limit, we need to randomize the discretization
times, and thus introduce an extra dimension, defining
$\Omega^*\define[0,1]\times\OmegaEd\times C_0^d\times C_0^{d^2}$.
Note that $\Omega^*$ can also be written as
$\Omega^{\sE^*,d^*}$, where $\sE^*=[0,1]\times\sE$
and $d^*=d+d+d^2$.  We denote $\sF^{\sE^*,d^*}$ simply
as $\sF^*$ and denote $\sF^{\sE^*,d^*}_t$ simply as $\sF^*_t$.
On $\sF^*$ we define the measure
$\Q$ to be the product of uniform measure on $[0,1]$
and the measure induced by $(Z_0,Y,B,C)$ under $\P$
on $\OmegaEd\times C_0^d\times C_0^{d^2}$.
The generic element of $\Omega^*$ will be denoted
$\omega=(\mu,\epsilon,\eta,\beta,\gamma)$,
and we define the projections
$$
U^*(\omega)=\mu,\,\,
Z_0^*(\omega)=\epsilon,\,\,
Y^*(\omega)=\eta,\,\,
B^*(\omega)=\beta,\,\,
C^*(\omega)=\gamma.
$$
On the filtered probability space
$(\Omega^*,\sF^*,\{\sF^*_t\}_{t\geq 0},\Q)$,
$Y^*$ is a semimartingale with characteristic pair
$(B^*, C^*)$.

We choose an $\R^d$-valued predictable process $b^*$
whose $i$-th component at each time $t>0$, denoted
$(b_i^*)_t$, agrees with
$$
\liminf_{k\rightarrow\infty}
k\big((B_i^*)_t-(B^*_i)_{(t-\frac{1}{k})^+}\big)
$$
whenever the latter is finite.
Likewise, we choose an $\R^{d^2}$-valued predictable process
$c^*$ whose $(i,j)$-th component at each time $t>0$,
denoted $(c_{i,j}^*)_t$, agrees with
$$
\liminf_{k\rightarrow\infty}
k\big((C_{i,j}^*)_t-(C^*_{i,j})_{(t-\frac{1}{k})^+}\big)
$$
whenever the latter is finite.
By assumption, the components of $B^*$
and $C^*$ are $\Q$-almost surely
absolutely continuous, and so their left derivatives
are defined for Lebesgue-almost every $t\geq0$, $\Q$-almost
surely.  By construction,
$b^*$ and $c^*$ are these left derivatives
whenever they are defined.  It follows that
\be\label{6.4}
\Q\left[\int_0^t\big(\|b^*_s\|+\|c^*_s\|\big)\,ds<\infty,
B^*_t=\int_0^tb^*_s\,ds,
C^*_t=\int_0^tc^*_s\,ds\,\,\forall t\right]=1.
\ee
For $i,j=1,\dots,d$, the sets
\bea
&&\hspace{-.4in}
\{t\in[0,\infty):\frac{\partial}{\partial t}(B_i^*)_t(\omega)
\mbox{ exists but is not equal to }(b_i^*)_t(\omega)\},
\label{6.4a}\\
&&\hspace{-.4in}
\{t\in[0,\infty):\frac{\partial}{\partial t}(C_{i,j}^*)_t(\omega)
\mbox{ exists but is not equal to }(c_{i,j}^*)_t(\omega)\}
\nonumber
\eea
are empty for {\em every} $\omega\in\Omega^*$.

We set $Z^*\define\Phi(Z_0^*,Y^*)$ and
observe that the random time $U^*$ is strongly independent of
$(Y^*,Z^*,B^*,C^*,b^*,c^*)$ (recall Definition \ref{D4.3}).
Furthermore, the distribution of $(Y^*,Z^*,B^*,C^*)$ under $\Q$
is the same as the distribution of $(Y,Z,B,C)$ under $\P$, so
\eqref{6.0} and \eqref{6.4} imply that
\be\label{6.45}
\E{\int_0^t f(Y_s, Z_s, b_s, c_s) \, ds}
= \E^{\Q} {\int_0^t f(Y^*_s, Z^*_s, b^*_s, c^*_s) \, ds}
\ee
for any $t \geq 0$ and $f$ such that one side of \eqref{6.45} is well defined.
In particular, \eqref{6.1} and \eqref{6.45} imply that
\be\label{6.5}
\E^{\Q}\left[\int_0^t\big(\|b_s^*\|+\|c_s^*\|\big)\,ds\right]<\infty,
\quad t\geq 0,
\ee
and \eqref{6.2}, \eqref{6.45}, and
Lemma~\ref{L4.2} ensure the existence of a
Lebesgue-null set $N^* \subset [0, \infty)$ such
that
$\bhat(t,Z_t^*)=\E^{\Q}[b_t^*\,|\,Z^*_t]$
and $\chat(t,Z_t^*)=\E^{\Q}[c_t^*\,|\,Z^*_t]$
for all $t\notin N^*$.
From (\ref{6.5}) and the conditional version of Jensen's inequality, we also have
$$
\E^{\Q}\left[\int_0^t\big(\|\bhat(s,Z_s^*)\|
+\|\chat(s,Z_s^*)\|\big)\,ds\right]<\infty,\quad t\geq 0,
$$
or equivalently,
$$
\E\left[\int_0^t\big(\|\bhat(s,Z_s)\|
+\|\chat(s,Z_s)\|\big)\,ds\right]<\infty,\quad t\geq 0.
$$

\noi
\underline{Step 2: Construction of extended partitions}.

For each positive integer $m$, set $N(m)=m^2$,
$T_0^m\define 0$, and for  $i=1,\dots,N(m)$, set
$T_i^m\define(U^*+i-1)/m$.  Note that each $T_i^m$
is $\sigma(U^*)$ measurable, and consequently
is an $\{\sF^*_t\}_{t\geq 0}$-stopping time.  Let $\Pi^m$
denote this set of stopping times.  The sequence
of random partitions $\{\Pi^m\}_{m=1}^{\infty}$
converges uniformly to the identity (Definition \ref{D5.6}).

For the next step, we adopt the notation
$X=(Y^*,B^*,C^*)$.
We set
$\sG_0^m=\sH_0^m=\sF_0^*=\sigma(U,Z_0^*)$,
and for $i=1,\dots,N(m)$, we set
$\sG_i^m=\sigma(U^*,Z^*_{T_i})$ and
$\sH_i^m=\sG_{i-1}^m\vee\sigma\big(
\Delta(X^{T_i^m},T_{i-1}^m)\big)$.
Finally, we set $T_{N(m)+1}^m=\infty$ and
$\sH_{N(m)+1}^m=
\sG_{N(m)}^m\vee\sigma
\big(\Delta(X,T_{N(m)}^m)\big)$.
It is clear that part
(a) of Definition \ref{D3.2} is
satisfied.  To show that
$(T_i^m,\sG_i^m)_{i=1}^{N(m)}$ is an extended partition,
it suffices to verify condition (b) of
Definition \ref{D3.2}, i.e., that $\sG_i^m\subset\sH_i^m$ for
$i=1,\dots,N(m)$.  In particular, it suffices to show
that $Z^*_{T_i^m}$ is measurable with respect to
$\sigma(U^*)\vee\sigma(Z^*_{T_{i-1}^m})
\vee\sigma(\Delta(X^{T_i^m},T_{i-1}^m))$.
Let $\tau\geq 0$ be a possibly random time and define
$S_i^m=(\tau-T_{i-1}^m)^+$.
On the set $T_{i-1}^m\leq \tau\leq T_i^m$, we may use
property (\ref{2.7}) of the updating function $\Phi$
to write
\bea
Z^*_{\tau}
&=&
\Theta_{S_i^m}\big(Z^*,T_{i-1}^m\big)\nonumber\\
&=&
\Theta_{S_i^m}\big(\Phi(Z_0^*,Y^*),T_{i-1}^m\big)\nonumber\\
&=&
\Phi_{S_i^m}\big(\Phi_{T_{i-1}^m}(Z_0^*,Y^*),
\Delta(Y^*,T_{i-1}^m)\big)\nonumber\\
&=&
\Phi_{S_i^m}\big(Z^*_{T_{i-1}^m},
\Delta(Y^*,T_{i-1}^m)\big).\label{6.10a}
\eea
If we take $\tau=T_i^m$, this leads to
$$
Z_{T_i^m}^*=
\Phi_{T_i^m-T_{i-1}^m}\big(Z^*_{T_{i-1}^m},
\Delta(Y^*,T_{i-1}^m)\big)
=\Phi_{T_i^m-T_{i-1}^m}^{T_i^m-T_{i-1}^m}\big(Z^*_{T_{i-1}^m},
\Delta(Y^*,T_{i-1}^m)\big),
$$
and by property (\ref{2.6}), the last expression depends on
the path of $\Delta(Y^*,T_{i-1}^m)$ only up to
time $T_i^m-T_{i-1}^m$, which agrees with the path
of $\Delta((Y^*)^{T_i^m},T_{i-1}^m)$ up to time
$T_i^m-T_{i-1}^m$.
We have thus written $Z^*_{T_i^m}$ in terms of
$T_i^m-T_{i-1}^m$, which is nonrandom unless $i=1$, in which
case it is $U^*/m$, in terms of $Z^*_{T_{i-1}^m}$,
and in terms of $\Delta((Y^*)^{T_i^m},T_{i-1}^m)$.

\vspace{\baselineskip}
\noi
\underline{Step 3: Concatenated measures}.

We denote by
$\Pi^m$ the extended partition
$(T_i^m,\sG_i^m)_{i=1}^{N(m)}$.
These extended partitions are on the
space $\Omega^*=[0,1]\times\OmegaEd\times C_0^d\times C_0^{d^2}$,
which is the same as $\Omega^{\sE^*,d^*}$ defined in Step 1.
Theorem \ref{T3.3} implies the existence
of concatenated measures $\Q^m\define\Q^{\otimes\Pi^m}$
that satisfy
\bea
\Q^m[A]&=&\Q[A],\quad A\in\sH_i^m,\,\,i=0,1,\dots,N(m)+1,
\label{6.11b}\\
\Q^m[B\,|\,\sF^*_{T_i^m}]
&=&
\Q[B\,|\,\sG_i^m],\quad B\in\sH_{i+1}^m,\,\,i=0,1,\dots,N(m).
\label{6.11c}
\eea
Applying Proposition \ref{P3.12} with $X=(Y^*,B^*,C^*)$,
we see that $Y^*$ is a semimartingale with
characteristic pair $(B^*,C^*)$ under each $\Q^m$.

\vspace{\baselineskip}
\noi
\underline{Step 4: Tightness and convergence}.

Corollary \ref{C3.11}(b) shows that the collection of measures
induced on $C_0^d\times C_0^{d^2}$ by $(B^*,C^*)$ under
$\{\Q^m\}_{m=1}^{\infty}$ is tight.  Theorem VI.4.18
of \cite{JS} (Rebolledo's criterion; see \cite{R}) then implies that
the collection of measures induced on $C_0^d$ by $Y^*$
under $\{\Q^m\}_{m=1}^{\infty}$ is tight.
Since $Z_0^*$ has the same distribution under every
$\Q^m$, the set of measures induced on $\OmegaEd$
by $(Z_0^*,Y^*)$ is likewise tight.  Passing to a convergent
subsequence if necessary, we obtain a limiting measure $\Phat$ on
$\OmegaEd$.  To simplify notation, we assume that
the passage to a subsequence is not necessary to obtain
convergence.  We denote the coordinate
mappings on $\OmegaEd$ by $\Zhat_0$ and $\Yhat$,
and we define $\Zhat=\Phi(\Zhat_0,\Yhat)$.  The Continuous
Mapping Theorem implies that the distributions of
$(Y^*,Z^*)$ on $C_0^d\times C^{\sE}$ under
the sequence of measures $\{\Q^m\}_{m=1}^{\infty}$
converge to the distribution of $(\Yhat,\Zhat)$
under $\Phat$, i.e.,
$\Q^m\circ(Y^*,Z^*)^{-1}
\Longrightarrow\Phat\circ(\Yhat,\Zhat)^{-1}$.

\vspace{\baselineskip}
\noi
\underline{Step 5: Agreement of one-dimensional distributions}.

Returning to (\ref{6.10a}), we take $\tau=t$, a fixed nonnegative
number, so that $S_i^m=(t-T_{i-1}^m)^+$.
On the $\sH_i^m$-measurable
set $\{T_{i-1}^m\leq t<T_i^m\}$, we have
$$
Z_t^*=
\Phi_{S_i^m}\big(Z^*_{T_{i-1}^m},\Delta(Y^*,T_{i-1}^m)\big),
$$
and the term
$\Phi_{S_i^m}\big(Z^*_{T_{i-1}^m},\Delta(Y^*,T_{i-1}^m)\big)$
restricted to $\{T_{i-1}^m\leq t<T_i^m\}$
depends only on $S_i^m$, $Z^*_{T_{i-1}^m}$, and
$\Delta((Y^*)^{T_i^m},T_{i-1}^m)$, all of which are
$\sH_i^m$-measurable.  Because $\Q^m$ and $\Q$ agree
on each $\sH_i^m$, we conclude that for every Borel
subset $A$ of $\sE$ and for every $t\geq 0$,
\bea
\Q^m[Z_t^*\in A]
&=&
\sum_{i=1}^{N(m)+1}\Q^m[Z^*_t\in A\mbox{ and }T_{i-1}^m\leq t<T_i^m]
\nonumber\\
&=&
\sum_{i=1}^{N(m)+1}
\Q[Z^*_t\in A\mbox{ and }T_{i-1}^m\leq t<T_i^m]\nonumber\\
&=&
\Q[Z_t^*\in A]
\,\,=\,\,
\P[Z_t\in A].\label{6.15a}
\eea
But the distributions of $Z^*$ under the sequence of measures
$\{\Q^m\}_{m=1}^{\infty}$ converge to the distribution
of $\Zhat$ under $\Phat$, and part (ii) of Theorem \ref{T6.1}
is proved.

\vspace{\baselineskip}
\noi
\underline{Step 6: Semimartingale characteristic of the limit}.

To complete the proof, we must show that under the
measure $\Phat$ on $\OmegaEd$,
$\Yhat$ is a semimartingale with characteristic pair
$(\Bhat,\Chat)$, defined in part (i) of Theorem \ref{T6.1}.
We do this by showing that the distribution
of the $(Y^*,Z^*,B^*,C^*)$ under $\Q^m$ converges to
the distribution of $(\Yhat,\Zhat,\Bhat,\Chat)$ under $\Phat$, i.e.,
\be\label{6.11}
\Q^m\circ(Y^*,Z^*,B^*,C^*)^{-1}\Longrightarrow
\Phat\circ(\Yhat,\Zhat,\Bhat,\Chat)^{-1}.
\ee
The filtration on $\OmegaEd$, defined at the beginning of
Section \ref{SConMea}, is generated by $\Yhat$.
Once (\ref{6.11}) is established,
Theorem IX.2.4 of \cite{JS} will give the desired result.

On $\Omega^*$ we define the processes
$$
\bbar_t\define\bhat(t,Z_t^*),\quad
\Bbar_t\define\int_0^t\bbar_s\,ds,\quad
\cbar_t\define\chat(t,Z_t^*),\quad
\Cbar_t\define\int_0^t\cbar_s\,ds,\quad t\geq 0.
$$
According to Proposition \ref{P5.2},
\bea
&&\Q^m\circ(Y^*,Z^*,\Bbar,\Cbar)^{-1}\Longrightarrow
\Phat\circ(\Yhat,\Zhat,\Bhat,\Chat)^{-1},\label{6.12}\\
&&\{\bbar,\lambda_{[0,t]}\times\Q^m\}_{m\in\N}\mbox{ is
uniformly integrable for every }t\in[0,\infty),\qquad\label{6.13}\\
&&\{\cbar,\lambda_{[0,t]}\times\Q^m\}_{m\in\N}\mbox{ is
uniformly integrable for every }t\in[0,\infty).\nonumber
\eea
We show that
$\Q^m\circ(Y^*,Z^*,B^*,C^*)^{-1}$
and $\Q^m\circ(Y^*,Z^*,\Bbar,\Cbar)^{-1}$
have the same limit as $m\rightarrow\infty$.
We do this by showing that
for every $\epsilon>0$ and $t\in[0,\infty)$,
\bea
\lim_{m\rightarrow\infty}\Q^m\left[\sup_{0\leq s\leq t}
\|B^*_s-\Bbar_s\|\geq \epsilon\right]&=&0,\label{6.16}\\
\lim_{m\rightarrow\infty}\Q^m\left[\sup_{0\leq s\leq t}
\|C^*_s-\Cbar_s\|\geq \epsilon\right]&=&0.\label{6.17}
\eea
Once this has been done, (\ref{6.12}) will imply (\ref{6.11}),
and we will be done.

\vspace{\baselineskip}
\noi
\underline{Step 7: Proof of (\ref{6.16}) and (\ref{6.17})}.

In fact, we prove only (\ref{6.16}), because the
proof of (\ref{6.17}) is the same.  Without loss of
generality, we assume that $B^*$ and $\Bhat$ are one-dimensional.

For $i=1,\dots,N(m)$, define the
$\sH_{i+1}^m$-measurable random variable
$$
\xi_i^m\define\liminf_{k\rightarrow \infty}
k(B^*_{T_i^m+\frac{1}{k}}-B^*_{T_i^m}),
$$
which is the right derivative of $B^*$ at $T_i^m$ whenever
this derivative is defined.  Recall from Step 1
that $b^*_{T_i^m}$ is the left
derivative of $B^*$ at $T_i^m$ whenever this derivative
is defined and is finite.  By construction, $B^*$ is independent of
$T_i^m$ under $\Q$, and its derivative is defined and is finite
Lebesgue-almost everywhere, $\Q$-almost surely.
But $T_i^m$ is uniformly distributed on
$[\frac{i-1}{n},\frac{i}{n}]$.  It follows that
\be\label{6.19}
\Q[\xi_i^m=b^*_{T_i^m}]=1,\quad i=1,\dots,N(m).
\ee

We define three sequences of step functions:
$$
b_t^m\define
\sum_{i=1}^{N(m)}
\xi_i^m\ind_{[T_i^m,T_{i+1}^m)}(t),\quad,
\bbar_t^m\define\sum_{i=1}^{N(m)}\bbar_{T_i^m}
\ind_{[T_i^m,T_{i+1}^m)},\quad
b_t^{\Pi^m}\define\sum_{i=1}^{N(m)}b_{T_i^n}^*
\ind_{[T_i^m,T_{i+1}^m)}.
$$
We further define
$$
B_t^m\define\int_0^tb_s^m\,ds,\quad
\Bbar_t^m\define\int_0^t\bbar_s^m\,ds.
$$
Because of (\ref{6.19}), $b^m$ and $b^{\Pi^m}$ are
$\Q$-indistinguishable.

Each $B^m$ is piecewise linear,
and so for {\em every} $\omega\in\Omega^*$,
$\frac{\partial}{\partial t}B_t^m(\omega)=b_t^m(\omega)$
except at finitely many values of $t$.
In addition, $\Delta(B^m,T_i^m)$ is
$\sigma(\xi_j^m:j\geq i)$-measurable.
For $j\geq i$, $\xi_j^m$ is
$\sH_{j+1}^m$-measurable,
and we have shown in the proof of Theorem
\ref{T3.3} (see (\ref{HinG}))
that $\sH_{j+1}^m\subset\sG_i^m\vee\sigma\big(\Delta(X,T_i^m)\big)$
for $j=i,i+1,\dots,N(m)$, so we may conclude that
$\Delta(B^m,T_i^m)$ is
$\sG_i^m\vee\sigma\big(\Delta(X,T_i^m)\big)$-measurable
for $i=1,\dots,N(m)$.
This measurability condition
is trivially satisfied when $i=0$ as well.
We conclude that the pair of processes
$(B^m, b^m)$ satisfies the hypotheses
of Proposition \ref{P3.10}, including (\ref{3.15}),
with $\Q$ replacing $\P$ and $\Q^m$ replacing $\P^{\otimes\Pi}$.

Because $B^*$ is a component of $X$ and the set
